ceqa-f67c9656255004e4c3.projectTitle: Notice of Mutual Agreement No. 2026-2; Approval of a Two-Year Term Extension for the Alameda Corridor Police and Security Services Agreement
ceqa-f67c9656255004e4c3.description: The Port of Long Beach, acting by and through its Harbor Commissioners (Port), approved Notice of Mutual Agreement (NMA) No. 2026-2 between the Port of Long Beach, Port of Los Angeles, Alameda Corridor Transportation Authority, Union Pacific Railroad (UP), and BNSF Railway. NMA No. 2026-2 approves a two-year extension of the Alameda Corridor Dispatch Agreement through October 14, 2028. The existing Dispatching Agreement between the Alameda Corridor Transportation Authority (ACTA), the BNSF Railway, and the Union Pacific Railroad (UP) has been in place since January 30, 2002 and is set to expire on October 14, 2026. ceqa-dc622075e29e5f4e7f.name: Pier J Zero Emissions Infrastructure Project – Harbor Development Permit No. 26-018
ceqa-dc622075e29e5f4e7f.projectTitle: Pier J Zero Emissions Infrastructure Project – Harbor Development Permit No. 26-018
ceqa-dc622075e29e5f4e7f.description: The Pier J Zero Emissions Infrastructure Project involves reconfiguration of four existing cargo-handling equipment and vehicle parking areas at the Pier J marine terminal to accommodate electrical infrastructure improvements and installation of a total of 313 electric charging stations for human-operated utility tractor rigs (UTR), top handlers, forklifts, on-terminal trucks (White Trucks), and personal operated vehicles (POV). A new SCE service transformer will be installed within the SCE Wharf Substation. Supporting electrical infrastructure for electrified cargo handling equipment consists of electric vehicle service equipment, underground conduits and conductors, new substations, switchgear, and transformers., and electric chargers. Ancillary improvements include parking lot repaving, traffic paving and lane improvements, installation of bollards and new markings for parking, traffic and pedestrian pathways. Construction activities would involve demolishing of existing small structures, removal of existing light poles, gutters, chain link fencing, other small ancillary traffic and parking related structures and the demolition of pavement totaling approximately 14,700 cubic yards of material. Approximately 8,850 cubic yards of pavement will be added to the project site. Construction of the project is expected to take approximately 12 months. The UTR Parking area will be reconfigured from the existing UTR Parking area with 130 new 200 kilowatt (kW) single-port electric chargers. At the northside of the area, Southern California Edison switchgear and secondary substations will serve as a connection point between the SCE Wharf Substation, new SCE transformer and the newly installed vehicle chargers. The parking area will be overlain with new asphalt and marked parking stalls. Throughout the area, there will be bollards, k-rails, curbs and wheel stops installed to provide physical boundaries from vehicle crossings. Traffic and pedestrian walkways will be marked to provide clear traffic flow and clear parking designations. Three canopy shade structures will be installed on the east side of the UTR Parking area that will serve as a point of check-in for employees before they walk westward into the parking area to access vehicles. Site circulation consists of two-lane drive aisles which lead to ingress and egress on the west end of the parking area. The White Truck and POV EV Charging Area (Site 1) will be reconfigured to accommodate a total of 145 white truck (work truck) parking stalls, 220 POV parking stalls, five standard parking stalls compliant with the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), and two van accessible ADA parking stalls. Fifty-two (52) stalls will accommodate dual dispenser Level 2 chargers for the works trucks; 12 stalls will have dual dispensing Level 2 chargers for POV. The electric chargers will be powered by connecting electrical lines with a series of conduit and pull boxes installed, to an SCE switcher south of the area. Throughout the parking area, new asphalt will be overlain, new traffic and parking striping will be marked and new curbs, bollards and wheel stops will be installed. A reinforced concrete traffic barrier (k-rail) will be installed to separate the POV and white truck parking areas and employees will access both areas via a turnstile. The k-rail barrier will separate the two areas in a division where POV parking will occupy the northern portion and white truck parking will occupy the southern portion. Ingress and egress of the site will be located on the east side of the area and two-way lanes will circulate throughout the parking areas. The White Truck and POV EV Charging Area (Site 2) will be reconfigured to accommodate a total of 125 white truck (work truck) parking stalls, 125 new POV parking stalls, four standard ADA parking stalls and one van accessible ADA parking stall. Out of the total 126 white truck parking stalls, 52 stalls will have dual dispenser Level 2 chargers. Out of the total 125 POV vehicle parking stalls, 22 will have dual dispensing Level 2 chargers. The parking area’s electric chargers’ cabling will connect to a switchboard on the west side of the area, which would then connect to the secondary substation located at the UTR Parking area and ultimately will connect to- and be powered by the SCE Wharf Substation, which provides power to the entire electric distribution of the project. New pavement will be overlain on the parking area and traffic, pedestrian and parking striping will be painted. Curbs, wheel stops and bollards will be installed to prevent vehicle crossover and provide protection to chargers and electrical equipment. K-rail along the westside portion of the parking area will enclose it completely from any entry. The center of the parking area will divide the area into east and west portions. The east portion of the parking area will have POV vehicle stalls and the west portion will have stalls for white trucks. On the east portion of the parking area, vehicle ingress and egress are available from the north and south sides with three available drive aisles. The west portion of the parking area will have ingress and egress from the southside with three available drive aisles that will also have k-rails to maintain clear paths for each drive aisle. The Top Handler Parking Area will be reconfigured to accommodate 42 future electrical top handlers and will be charged with single dispenser 200 kW Level 3 chargers, where each top handler will have its own dedicated stall and charger. The chargers will be powered by connection to a secondary substation southeast of the parking area, which will then connect to the primary SCE Wharf Substation, which provides power to the entire electric distribution of the project. There will also be 10 parking spaces are provided for 10kW light-duty forklift chargers, and 6 parking spaces are provided for 20kW heavy-duty forklift chargers. New pavement will be overlain on the parking area and traffic, pedestrian and parking striping will be painted. K-rails will also be provided around the walkways for additional pedestrian safety. Each parking stall is sized to locate the EV charger outside of the boom area and wheel stops will be provided to prevent the vehicle from pulling too far into the stall. A four feet walkway will be provided between each parking stall for additional user safety. A shaded canopy structure will be placed northeast of the parking area and will serve as an area for vehicle check-in, where workers will proceed to pick up their respective vehicles in the parking area, immediately east of the check-in area. A center drive aisle separates the parking area in a manner where parking stalls are located on the east, west and north edges of the parking area. Ingress and egress are available from the south side of the parking area.

ceqa-d4115a5fed4ad2b3a6.agency: Los Angeles Department of Water and Power
ceqa-d4115a5fed4ad2b3a6.agencyName: Los Angeles Department of Water and Power
ceqa-d4115a5fed4ad2b3a6.description: The Substation Program consists of planned developments and conceptual improvements to the LADWP distribution system through the planning horizon year 2045. To keep pace with the City’s growing electricity needs and reduce strain on the existing system, LADWP proposes to modernize its distribution system by constructing four new distributing substations to serve the Sun Valley, Silver Lake, Southeast Los Angeles, and Wilmington areas, and improving existing distributing substations and receiving substations. These improvements would take place in the LADWP in-basin service area, which covers the City of Los Angeles, and focus on relieving overloaded facilities, modernizing aging equipment, and meeting the City’s growing electricity needs to ensure reliable power delivery into the future.

ceqa-380e4434193e1f4648.name: City of Inglewood General Plan Update

ceqa-380e4434193e1f4648.description: The City of Inglewood is proposing a comprehensive General Plan Update (IGPU), which expands the planning horizon to 2050. The City’s last comprehensive General Plan update was completed in 1987, although individual elements have been amended since that time. The proposed IGPU would address all State requirements and would include the following nine elements: Circulation, Conservation, Economic Development (new element), Environmental Justice, Housing, Land Use, Noise, Open Space, and Safety. The Draft Program Environmental Impact Report will evaluate the reasonably foreseeable environmental effects associated with implementation of the proposed General Plan Update, including development that could occur under the proposed Land Use Plan and implementation of the goals, policies, and programs contained in the updated General Plan elements.

ceqa-e588e5e50bf2800831.description: The 3-acre Pamela County Park (Park) features picnic areas, basketball courts, a skate park, a community building, a gymnasium, and multi-use fields. The community building hosts a variety of activities and classes for children, teens, adults, and seniors, including EveryBody Plays after-school programs, OurSPOT teen programs, Women’s Group support network events, seasonal arts and culture events, and youth, teen, and senior nutrition programs. The proposed project scope includes replacement of the community building roof, existing play area safety surfacing, skate park equipment, and light fixtures, as well as related site improvements.

ceqa-9ecc70a693cd9c1087.description: The 9.6-acre Rimgrove Park includes a splash pad, playground, basketball court, softball fields, outdoor fitness equipment, picnic shade structures, community buildings, restrooms, and a parking lot. A number of these amenities are in need of repair or replacement. The roof-mounted heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) package unit serving the Tiny Tots building is outdated and no longer functional, the outdoor fitness equipment is worn and dilapidated, and the wooden picnic shade structures are weathered and deteriorating. The proposed project scope includes replacement of the roof-mounted HVAC package unit; replacement of outdoor fitness equipment; installation of shade trees to replace standing dead or dying trees; replacement of one existing picnic shade structure; and related site improvements.

ceqa-a2d8250f435041cb55.name: Lennox Park Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning (HVAC) and Roof Project
ceqa-a2d8250f435041cb55.projectTitle: Lennox Park Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning (HVAC) and Roof Project
ceqa-a2d8250f435041cb55.agency: Los Angeles County Department of Parks & Recreation
ceqa-a2d8250f435041cb55.description: Lennox Park is a 6-acre park that provides a variety of recreational facilities, including a swimming pool; a community building that houses a gymnasium and multipurpose room; a softball field; a basketball court; a teen center; a senior center; futsal courts; and a fitness zone. According to the 2016 Los Angeles Countywide Parks Needs Assessment, Lennox Park is located in a study area with a very high park need. The heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) systems serving the community building and senior center have exceeded their useful service lives, making them unreliable, inefficient, and unable to adequately meet the needs of either facility. In addition, the roof of the community building shows signs of age and wear, including leaks and compromised insulation. Replacement of these essential building systems is necessary to improve energy efficiency and provide a safe and comfortable environment for daily activities. The improvements also serve an important public safety function. Because the community building is officially designated as a cooling center, modernizing this infrastructure is critical to supporting community health and resilience during periods of extreme heat. The proposed project will replace the existing roof of the community building and replace the HVAC systems serving both the community building and senior center.

ceqa-1b9ccc3bf001bec452.name: Early Intervention for Invasive Ailanthus altissima in Angeles National Forest Watersheds
ceqa-1b9ccc3bf001bec452.projectTitle: Early Intervention for Invasive Ailanthus altissima in Angeles National Forest Watersheds
ceqa-1b9ccc3bf001bec452.description: Agriculture Access has spent a number of years observing, monitoring, and hiking within the Texas Canyon watershed. Based on communications with both the Angeles National Forest and the Mountain Recreation and Conservation Authority (MRCA), who jointly own and manage portions of the Texas Canyon watershed, it seems likely that conservation of this watershed region is a high priority. Therefore, an investment in an invasive weed control project for the control and prevention of Tree of Heaven populations makes common sense over the long-term. By targeting both the largest ‘parent trees’ (having the tallest, most mature leaf canopies) and newest ‘root sprouts’ (having the most active growing leaf canopies) within this half-acre site, the project proposes to “suppress photosynthesis” and its “source-sink” relationship. By selecting the use of Integrated Pest Management (IPM) protocols that remove large parent canopies and root sprouts, and “block sunlight” over periods of 3-6 months to prevent their regrowth, the control of this invasive weed site will be achieved. Without sufficient sunlight, Tree of Heaven is unable to assimilate carbohydrates and distribute them to newly growing root sprouts. Thus, severely hindering new growth or expansion of the weed site. The main advantage of early intervention of Tree of Heaven weed sites, is that the population size is small (<1.0 acre), is thus is economically feasible and efficient to control and manage over the long-term. If by controlling photosynthesis within leaves, crowns, and root sprouts of this Tree of Heaven weed site at an early-intervention stage of development, then it should be feasible to stop the expansion, and arrest the growth of the entire site within the Texas Canyon Watershed.

The Project will not cause an increase in student capacity or enrollment and would not result in an increase in the intensity of use. ceqa-0a85b726da6ff1f1d6.description: The California Department of Fish and Wildlife is issuing a western Joshua tree hazard management permit to Bible Holiness Church (Permit No. 1927-HMP-2026-298) pursuant to Fish and Game Code section 1927.4 for a project to trim and remove one hazardous living western Joshua tree. The trimming and removal of the living western Joshua tree specifically authorized under this Permit shall not disturb the root ball or sprouting western Joshua tree at the base. Western Joshua tree hazard management permits are issued to property owners for the purpose of removing or trimming a dead western Joshua tree or trimming a living western Joshua tree, provided that the dead western Joshua tree or any limb to be removed meet one of the following conditions: (A) has fallen over and is within 30 feet of a structure; (B) is leaning against an existing structure; or (C) creates an imminent threat to public health or safety.

ceqa-aeec78e7e0af306992.agency: South Coast Air Quality Management District
ceqa-aeec78e7e0af306992.agencyName: South Coast Air Quality Management District
ceqa-aeec78e7e0af306992.description: Rule 461 was adopted to control emissions of volatile organic compounds and toxic air contaminants from gasoline dispensing facilities. Rule 461 currently has an alternative compliance option which allows operators of non-retail gasoline dispensing facilities (GDFs) to dispense gasoline into motor vehicles without requiring the use of California Air Resources Board-certified Phase II Enhanced Vapor Recovery systems, provided that the motor vehicles are equipped with Onboard Refueling Vapor Recovery (ORVR) systems and are owned or directly controlled by the facility operator. Proposed Amended Rule (PAR) 461 will streamline recordkeeping requirements for operators of non-retail GDFs whose fleets consist exclusively of ORVR-equipped motor vehicles by adding an option to allow documentation of total daily fuel dispensing quantities in aggregate, in lieu of the current requirement to record the amount of fuel dispensed on a per vehicle basis. PAR 461 will also include an editorial correction and remove an outdated provision which has been superseded by state reporting requirements. While no emission reductions are expected, increasing the options available in PAR 461 for fleet operators to demonstrate compliance with the recordkeeping provisions will benefit stakeholders by providing flexibility and improved clarity for implementing the applicable requirements while reducing the administrative workload.

ceqa-3087942ad207c410e4.name: Proposed Amended Rule 1157 – PM10 Emission Reductions from Aggregate and Related Operations
ceqa-3087942ad207c410e4.projectTitle: Proposed Amended Rule 1157 – PM10 Emission Reductions from Aggregate and Related Operations
ceqa-3087942ad207c410e4.agency: South Coast Air Quality Management District
ceqa-3087942ad207c410e4.agencyName: South Coast Air Quality Management District
ceqa-3087942ad207c410e4.description: Rule 1157 regulates aggregate and related operations to reduce emissions of particulate matter with an aerodynamic diameter of 10 microns or less (PM10). Proposed Amended Rule 1157 (PAR 1157) will further reduce PM10 emissions from aggregate and related operations by: 1) expanding the applicability to include construction and demolition debris transfer stations; 2) specifying frequencies for when the application of dust control/suppressants or chemical stabilizers are required; 3) adding new compliance pathway for conducting periodic inspections of open storage piles in lieu of prescribed dust suppressant application frequencies; 4) adding enhanced recordkeeping requirements; 5) adding new requirements to standardize signage for applicable facilities; 6) expanding requirements that are triggered by recurring violations; and 7) removing obsolete requirements. Implementation of PAR 1157 will require installation of new signage for all applicable facilities and may require the installation of rumble grates and gravel pads at some facilities. Implementing additional requirements applicable to aggregate and related operations to reduce PM10 emissions and address community concerns will improve compliance which will benefit public health and ambient air quality.

ceqa-06d4f441814fd701a9.description: On July 21, 2026, the Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors (Board), approved a proposed five-year lease and authorized the Chief Executive Officer (CEO) to execute the lease for a 16,488-square-foot medical space located at 1700 Zonal Avenue, Ste B, in Los Angeles. The lease is with Los Angeles Centers for Alcohol and Drug Abuse (L.A. CADA) for the operation of a residential withdrawal management facility that will support clients in stabilizing withdrawal symptoms and serve as a pathway to further treatment _services. L.A. CADA will offer a set of treatment interventions, as a short­-term residential facility, aimed at medical and clinical management, stabilization of acute intoxication, and withdrawal from alcohol and other substances. The Lease is within the scope of the development per the Final EIR dated, November 18, 2014, for the LAC+USC Medical Center Campus Master Plan (State Clearinghouse 2014051061 ). The Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors adopted Findings of Fact (Findings) and a Statement of Overriding Considerations (SOC) and a Mitigation Monitoring and Reporting Program (MMRP). On December 19, 2017, the Board certified the First Addendum to the EIR and approved a 64-bed Crisis Residential Care Center on the LAC+USC campus. The Second Addendum to the certified EIR further analyzed impacts of the revisions to the Campus Master Plan related to the Psychiatric Subacute Facility, Mental Health Urgent Care and Residential Withdrawal Management Facility and determined that none of the conditions that would require preparation of a subsequent EIR exist. The adopted findings, SOC and MMRP will continue to apply. Since the time of certification of the addendum, there have been no changes to the RWMF or to the circumstances under which the RWMF is undertaken that require further review or findings under CEQA. This NOD states that the County certified the Final EIR, adopted CEQA Findings of Fact, adopted a Mitigation Monitoring and Reporting Program (MMRP), and adopted a Statement of Overriding Considerations for significant environmental impacts that could not be fully mitigated. The filing further confirms that mitigation measures were incorporated into the project and that the environmental review documents are available for public review through Los Angeles County.

ceqa-9fd3411ad2cc645ab6.name: Emergency Permit for Management of Hazardous Waste, World Oil Environmental Services, Compton, California
ceqa-9fd3411ad2cc645ab6.projectTitle: Emergency Permit for Management of Hazardous Waste, World Oil Environmental Services, Compton, California
ceqa-9fd3411ad2cc645ab6.agency: California Department of Toxic Substances Control
ceqa-9fd3411ad2cc645ab6.description: The California Department of Toxic Substances Control (DTSC), pursuant to authority granted under California Code of Regulations (CCR), Title 22, Division 4.5, Chapter 20, Sec. 66270.61, has issued an Emergency Permit to World Oil Environmental Services (EPA ID# CAD028277036) to allow for storage of a Toxic Substance Control Act (TSCA) waste greater than ten (10) days. Specifically, Truck #1111 containing 1,380 gallons of used oil and 680 gallons of used antifreeze that is contaminated with polychlorinated biphenyl (PCB) will be stored at the Facility until an authorized facility can accept it. The contaminated used oil and used antifreeze is currently stored at 1300 Santa Fe Avenue, Compton, California 90221. Background: The generator’s samples of Truck #1014 resulted in a polychlorinated biphenyl (PCB) concentration of 4.7 parts per million (ppm). When Truck #1014 was in receiving at World Oil Environmental Services, the PCB concentration was found to have a concentration greater than 5 ppm. This classified the oily water as a TSCA hazardous waste. World Oil Environmental Services does not have a permit to manage the TSCA hazardous waste and is waiting to schedule an appointment with the Clean Harbors Aragonite Facility to deliver the truck. Project Activities: The contaminated oily water will be stored in a manner that is protective of the environment by implementing the following controls: • The truck must remain parked within the secondary containment system under tarps until the truck is transported to an authorized facility. • To prevent risk to the public, public access is restricted during storage of the truck. • Movement and storage of the truck will be in accordance with established standards. • The truck will be transported to an authorized facility where the TSCA hazardous waste will be offloaded, the truck will be decontaminated, and waste generated during decontamination will be managed by an authorized facility. Within 10 business days of the expiration of this permit, World Oil Environmental Services will submit a final report, signed in accordance with Title 22, CCR Sec. 66270.11(d). The report shall include certification that the treatment area has been cleared of all residual hazardous waste generated from this emergency treatment and all generated waste has been properly managed. The Emergency Permit is effective beginning Marcy 27, 2026, and shall expire on June 25, 2026.

ceqa-18d55f061ff4302685.name: Dockweiler Least Tern Fence Project
ceqa-18d55f061ff4302685.agency: California Department of Parks and Recreation
ceqa-18d55f061ff4302685.description: Dockweiler SB is host to a federally endangered California least tern colony. In the mid 1980’s, a portion of the beach northwest of Ballona Creek was enclosed to prevent human activity and ground based predators from disturbing the colony. In 2006 the enclosed area was expanded to its current footprint and a new fence was installed. The fencing material is in an advanced state of deterioration. Gaps in the mesh and collapse of arm wires has allowed humans and predators to easily access the colony, and related disturbance is associate with colony abandonment in 2022. Grant funding for Angeles District to replace the existing fence was obtained in 2023. A contractor will replace ~2,500 linear feet of chain link fencing protecting the ~7.5 acre California least tern colony, using heavy equipment and augering new post holes to a depth of ~4’.

Specifically, the existing open concrete channel will be replaced with a subsurface reinforced box culvert and a diversion structure designed to capture dry-weather flows and a portion of wet-weather flows. Captured stormwater will be conveyed to a treatment system consisting of pretreatment facilities and a vegetated bio-swale with a footprint of approximately 0.3 acres, a ponding depth of 0.75 feet, and a storage capacity of approximately 0.23 acre-feet. The bio-swale will include a subsurface passive irrigation system to support vegetation. The Project also includes construction of a shared use path above the culvert, raised crosswalks at Merced Avenue and Brockway Street, pedestrian gates, motion-activated lighting, and installation of an 8-foot-tall metal screening fence along both the southern and northern boundaries. The Project site is approximately 2.56 acres in size and is located within a fully developed urban area. Construction is anticipated to begin in May 2027 and be completed by December 2028.

ceqa-3c1ecca56779c96da7.name: C-4 Well site re-design and water treatment design
ceqa-3c1ecca56779c96da7.projectTitle: C-4 Well site re-design and water treatment design
ceqa-3c1ecca56779c96da7.description: The project consists of the design and construction of a new groundwater treatment system and a well at the City’s existing C-4 Well site. The project will enable the City to treat constituents detected in groundwater produced by the C-4 Well and return the well to beneficial use while ensuring that water delivered to consumers meets applicable state and federal drinking water standards. The treatment system will address PFOS, as well as manganese and arsenic. PFOS has been detected in groundwater produced from the C-4 Well and is now subject to increasingly stringent regulatory requirements. As a result, the C-4 Well cannot be operated for potable water supply without appropriate treatment. The proposed improvements will include treatment tanks and associated filtration equipment, piping, a chlorination/disinfection facility, and related electrical, SCADA, instrumentation, and water-quality monitoring equipment. A portion of the existing block wall at the well site will also be reconfigured to accommodate and enclose the additional treatment equipment. The project will utilize the existing C-4 Well site and will not require development of a new well site. The C-4 Well is permitted by the California Division of Drinking Water (DDW) to produce approximately 3,500 gallons per minute (gpm). The project does not propose to increase the well’s permitted production capacity; rather, it will provide the treatment necessary to allow the existing well to operate in compliance with applicable drinking water requirements.The project involves improvements to an existing facility and is intended to maintain and improve the reliability and quality of an existing public water supply. The project is therefore proposed to be categorically exempt from CEQA pursuant to State CEQA Guidelines Section 15301 (Class 1), Existing Facilities, which applies to minor alteration of existing structures, facilities, mechanical equipment, or topographical features involving negligible or no expansion of existing or former use.

ceqa-75cc852beb4942762d.name: 4505 West Prospect Avenue (ENV-2025-7076-CE)
ceqa-75cc852beb4942762d.description: The proposed project is for the demolition of two (2), one-story single-family dwellings, and the construction, use and maintenance of a three (3)-story, 15-unit residential building measuring 36 feet in height. The project is setting aside 10 percent of the total 15 units and a minimum of 13 percent of the total 15 units, respectively, for a total of two (2) Extremely Low-Income Household units. The building will contain 8,815 square feet of floor area with a 1.31:1 FAR. The unit mix will be comprised of eight (8) one-bedroom units, six (6) two-bedroom units, and one (1) threebedroom unit. There will be six (6) parking spaces with no guest parking spaces within the dedicated parking garage located at ground level. The proposed project also includes four (4) bicycle parking spaces, and 1,013.8 square feet of usable open space. Also, the proposed project is includes a cut and export of approximately 66.7 cubic yards, and an overexcavation/recompaction 468 cubic yards. ceqa-25faecbad1b94b8ea0.name: Environmental Impact Report Addendum (EIR State Clearinghouse No. 2013091009) for the North Lake Specific Plan (NLSP)
ceqa-25faecbad1b94b8ea0.description: The purpose of this Addendum to the Pasadena General Plan Environmental Impact Report (GP EIR) is to evaluate the environmental effects associated with the proposed NLSP Update and to determine whether these impacts are consistent with the evaluation presented in the GP EIR in compliance with CEQA (Public Resource Code Sections 21000 et seq.) and the State CEQA Guidelines (California Code of Regulations Section 15000 et seq.). The proposed project would update the NLSP to implement the Pasadena General Plan (General Plan). This project proposes to update the following components of the NLSP to bring it into alignment with the General Plan: • Specific Plan Area boundary • Vision, objectives, goals and policies • Zoning districts regulating allowed land uses • Density and intensity of development • Height and/or overall scale of buildings and structures • Distance of buildings and structures to the property line (setbacks/stepbacks) • Urban design standards • Vehicle access and parking standards • Types and amount of open space and landscaping requirements • Public realm standards (sidewalks, parkways and street trees) • Implementation programs The NLSP sets out a plan to facilitate investment, development, and improvements to the Plan Area, that will ultimately help realize the community's vision for North Lake Avenue. The NLSP optimizes land uses to increase opportunities for financially feasible commercial and residential developments, and help ensure that new development, sidewalk improvements, and added amenities contribute positively to the pedestrian experience. It also includes standards to protect historic resources and support existing elements of the area that provide a sense of place and distinct character, while providing contextual standards for new development. Future redevelopment opportunities will focus on infill development and making incremental changes to the area's built environment and land use mix. This document will be used by property and business owners, grant-seeking nonprofits, developers, decision makers, and City staff as the regulations that will guide private and public development projects. While the specific plan introduces a framework and toolkit for designing and implementing future developments, it does not mandate or accelerate any specific projects or immediate changes to the built environment. The General Plan leaves the more detailed development and design standards to be identified in the Specific Plan. The NLSP establishes the regulatory tools needed to implement the General Plan through the identification of development and design standards suited to the NLSP area. An EIR was prepared for the General Plan in compliance with CEQA and adopted by the City Council on August 17, 2015. This addendum to the General Plan EIR has been prepared to compare the environmental impacts of the proposed NLSP Update to those analyzed in the GP EIR.

ceqa-46d2f0490626d3b2af.name: 4034 North Verdugo Road (ENV-2025-7066-CE)
ceqa-46d2f0490626d3b2af.description: The project is for the change of use from a 937 square-foot business/residence to a 1,988 square-foot preschool, the demolition of 663 square feet of the existing building, and the construction of a two (2)-story addition, for a total building floor area of 1,988 square feet, with four (4) vehicle parking spaces. The project requires five (5) cubic yards of fill. The project site does not contain any Protected Trees or Shrubs. There is one (1) tree in the adjacent public right-of-way that will be maintained. The building will have a maximum building height of 29 feet and two (2) inches. The project requires the following: 1. Pursuant to LAMC Chapter 1, Section 13.08 and the Cypress Park and Glassell Park Community Design Overlay (CDO), a CDO Director’s Determination for the change of use from a 937 square-foot business/residence to a 1,988 square-foot preschool, the demolition of 663 square feet of the existing building, and the construction of a two (2)-story addition, for a total building floor area of 1,988 square feet. The project is located within the Northeast Los Angeles Community Plan which designates the project site for Neighborhood Commercial land uses with corresponding zones of C1, C1.5, C2, C4, and RAS3. The project site is zoned [Q]C1.5-1VL-CDO. The project is consistent with the applicable general plan land use designation and all applicable general plan policies as well as with the applicable zoning designation and regulations. The project site is wholly within the City of Los Angeles, on a site that is approximately 0.12 acres in size. Lots adjacent to the project site are developed with the following urban uses: commercial, single-family, and multi-family developments. The site is currently developed with a business/residence and the new use will be a preschool. The site is surrounded by development and therefore is not, and has no value as, a habitat for endangered, rare or threatened species. In addition, there are zero (0) Protected Trees on-site. The project will be subject to Regulatory Compliance Measures (RCMs), which require compliance with the City of Los Angeles Noise Ordinance, pollutant discharge, dewatering, stormwater mitigations; and Best Management Practices for stormwater runoff. These RCMs will ensure the project will not have significant impacts on noise and water. Furthermore, the project does not exceed the threshold criteria established by LADOT for preparing a transportation study. Interim thresholds were developed by DCP staff based on CalEEMod model runs relying on reasonable assumptions, consulting with AQMD staff, and surveying published air quality studies for which criteria air pollutants did not exceed the established SCAQMD construction and operational thresholds. The project site will be adequately served by all public utilities and services given that the change of use from a one (1)-story business/residence to a two (2)-story preschool totaling 1,988 square feet, with four (4) automobile parking spaces, will be on a site that has been previously developed and is consistent with the General Plan. Therefore, the project meets all of the Criteria for the Class 32.

ceqa-3eed356d91a49c6505.description: [Project Title Continued]: Around Designated Stops in the City of Burbank The City of Burbank publicly announces the initiation of the preparation of an Environmental Impact Report (EIR) for the Transit Oriented Development (TOD) Station Zoning (proposed project) pursuant to the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). The City of Burbank is the lead agency for the preparation of the EIR under CEQA because SCAG has elected not to conduct CEQA review on its SB 79 TOD zoning maps, and the City must do so to implement the SB 79 TOD zoning. As a result, the lots designated by SB 79 will be subject to state mandated height, FAR, and density requirements that exceed the City’s General Plan (Burbank2035) and Burbank Municipal Code (BMC) Title 10 (Zoning Regulation) requirements but have yet to be studied either by Metro in its 2022 project FEIR or SCAG prior to adopting SB 79 TOD Station Zoning maps. SCAG adopted SB 79 TOD Station Zoning maps on July 2, 2026.

ceqa-8b5742b7eef17e4135.name: Cost Share Agreement Between City of Long Beach and City of Los Angeles for Environmental Services at Long Beach Leads Extension Parcels LBX/MY-851 and LBX/SE-8
ceqa-8b5742b7eef17e4135.projectTitle: Cost Share Agreement Between City of Long Beach and City of Los Angeles for Environmental Services at Long Beach Leads Extension Parcels LBX/MY-851 and LBX/SE-8
ceqa-8b5742b7eef17e4135.description: The proposed action approves a cost share agreement with the City of Los Angeles for environmental services at Long Beach Leads Extension Parcels LBX/MY-851 and LBX/SE-853, including historical and future costs in an amount not to exceed $1,100,000, with a term commencing on the date of agreement signature through October 31, 2030. The Cities of Long Beach and Los Angeles have jointly owned LBX/MY-851 and LBX/SE-853 since 1994 and 2020, respectively. Both parcels are under regulatory oversight by the Los Angeles Regional Water Quality Control Board, which requires groundwater monitoring, free product recovery, and remediation of soil and groundwater. The Port of Los Angeles (POLA) has managed the environmental regulatory responsibilities since 2007. The agreement allows the Port of Long Beach (POLB) to reimburse the POLA for previous testing, monitoring, reporting, and remediation actions, and establishes a cost share arrangement between POLB and POLA for environmental work to be performed through October 31, 2030.

ceqa-c0fc94211ed8dbe400.name: Underground Cable Resilience Retrofit Project
ceqa-c0fc94211ed8dbe400.description: This project will replace approximately 30 miles of 34.5kV and 4.8kV underground cable in the project area over the course of five years. These upgrades will replace aging underground infrastructure, including equipment that is past its service life and at a risk of failure. By expediting the replacement of underground infrastructure, the project will increase energy flow capacity without increasing generation capacity and will reduce vulnerability to extreme weather conditions such as heatwaves and storms, improving overall energy reliability.

ceqa-67ba202c1c385b0233.name: Burbank Grid Forward
ceqa-67ba202c1c385b0233.description: This project will upgrade approximately 30 circuit miles of Burbank service territory’s distribution lines from 4kV to 12kV. It also will install supporting components including poles and transformers, as well as additional grid hardening equipment such as switchgear, protective relays, vaults, and conduit systems. By upgrading aging distribution lines, the project will reduce the frequency and duration of load-induced outages, decrease line losses, and increase the efficiency of energy delivery across the city. This grid modernizing measure strengthens the system's ability to withstand and quickly recover from disruptive weather events. California Energy Commission agreement number: CER-26-001.

ceqa-453df3d717927e819b.name: Bridgeport Elementary School Asphalt Play Courts Project
ceqa-453df3d717927e819b.projectTitle: Bridgeport Elementary School Asphalt Play Courts Project
ceqa-453df3d717927e819b.description: The proposed project will include improvements on approximately 1.08 acres of the Bridgeport ES campus. The proposed project will include the removal and replacement of existing asphalt located at the play area on the southeastern corner of the campus. The new asphalt surface will be restriped to include three basketball courts, three ball walls, two 4-square courts, four tetherball courts, and other various play markings. The gutters and drainage inlets within the project area will be removed and replaced. Seven tetherball posts will be removed, and four new tetherball posts will be installed. Two wooden ball walls will be removed and replaced with three new concrete masonry unit (CMU) ball walls. Existing basketball posts will remain in place. All underground utilities and associated infrastructure will remain. The project will also include the construction of a new concrete walkway around the perimeter of the play area. In addition, minor interior improvements will be made to the restrooms within Building A, consisting of upgrades to plumbing fixtures and accessories. The proposed project will include upgrades to the play structure area. Improvements will consist of the removal and replacement of the existing play structure, swings, and rubberized play surfacing. The existing concrete curbing will be extended. A new 4,800-square-foot shade structure will be installed above the play structure. Construction of the proposed project will be completed in two phases. The replacement of the asphalt and play equipment will occur between June and July 2027. The installation of the shade structure and rubber surfacing will be completed in August 2027. All construction equipment and workers will be staged within the boundaries of the project site, and contractors will adhere to Santa Clarita Municipal Code Section 11.44.080, Special Noise Sources: Construction and Building, to avoid disruption to campus operations. The proposed project will not increase the school's student capacity. All project improvements will be on campus, and no off-site improvements will be part of the proposed project.

ceqa-c3c1114028c1ee4fe1.description: The Westoria Residential Project proposes to demolish the three existing buildings (totaling 242,965 square feet) and the development of 335 residential units on 7.82 acres in the City of Torrance. The residential units would be developed within two sub-areas: Lot A would be developed with 98 four-story townhome units, and Lot B would feature 237 multifamily units within a six-story building with a maximum height of 80 feet and 5 inches. The Project would result in an average net density of 42.8 dwelling units per acre (du/ac) across the Project site. The Project also proposes an internal access drive, a subterranean parking garage, guest parking within drive aisles, recreational common space areas for resident use, ornamental landscaping, and additional stormwater and utility improvements to accommodate proposed residences. The Project would also include construction of two driveway entrances, one from Torrance Boulevard and one from S Western Avenue.

ceqa-d38fdbbb3b28aa1dbf.agency: California Department of Fish and Wildlife, South Coast Region 5
ceqa-d38fdbbb3b28aa1dbf.agencyName: Fish and Wildlife, Region 5 - South Coast, San Diego
ceqa-d38fdbbb3b28aa1dbf.description: The California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) issued this Restoration Management Permit (RMP) pursuant to section 1670 of the Fish and Game Code to the Environmental Restoration Group, LLC as represented by Debra Sharpton. The Project includes management or propagation activities intended to benefit native fish, wildlife, plants, or their habitat, or a combination thereof. The Project is expected to increase populations of California red-legged frog (Rana draytonii) and arroyo chub (Gila orcuttii) by removing the threat of predation by Louisiana red-swamp crayfish (Procambarus clarkii), an aquatic invasive species, and competition for food sources. In addition, terrestrial revegetation will provide greater nesting habitat for least Bell’s vireo (Vireo bellii pusillus). CDFW has determined that the Project is a Qualifying Restoration Project pursuant to section 1671(d)(1) of the Fish and Game Code, and the Project is expected to result in a substantial, cumulative benefit to native wildlife, plants, and their habitat. This notice is to advise that CDFW issued the above-described RMP on the date signed below.

ceqa-9c7f6d638f28aef87a.description: The proposed project involves construction of a groundwater well and water line which will connect to existing QHWD infrastructure. The proposed water line will be approximately 100 feet long and will be constructed in the existing road right of way. The well will be constructed on a previously graded residential lot. Work will include site preparation, mobilization of drilling equipment, drilling, and installation of well casings and screened intervals at depths appropriate to site-specific hydrogeologic conditions. Portable sound walls will be installed around drilling equipment to reduce noise transmission toward nearby residential areas and office buildings across the street. The purpose of the project is to improve water quality and achieve Division of Drinking Water regulatory compliance by blending with two existing wells. There are no long-term safety concerns associated with the proposed action. Temporary construction-related effects will be minimized through standard best management practices.

ceqa-7c80b6e0b7d270b845.name: 1537 S. Hayworth (New Condominiums) ENV-2025-5561-CE
ceqa-7c80b6e0b7d270b845.description: The Applicant proposes a Tentative Tract Map to merge two (2) existing lots into one (1) ground lot resulting in total lot area of approximately 13,761 square-feet, for the purpose of 30 new condominiums in a proposed multi-family residential building. On October 17, 2024, the Department of City Planning issued a Class 32 Categorical Exemption (ENV-20205018-CE) to permit the demolition of two (2) existing single-family dwellings and two (2) detached garages, and the construction, use and maintenance of a five (5)-story multifamily residential building containing 30 dwelling units, including three (3) units restricted to Extremely Low Income Households, in conjunction with an approval for the Transit Oriented Communities Affordable Housing Incentive Program (Case No. DIR-2020-5017-TOC-HCA). The project site is located at 1537-1541 South Hayworth Avenue within the Wilshire Community Plan. The proposed project is 57 feet in height and comprises 38,499 square feet of floor area. Demolition permits for the existing improvements were issued on August 27, 2024; however, at the time of writing, demolition had not yet begun. A building permit for the multi-family building was issued on March 5, 2026; however, at the time of writing, construction had not yet begun. The project proposes the cut and export of 9,682 (12,064 with a 25-percent swell factor) cubic yards of soil and the fill of 31 cubic yards. No import of soil is proposed. The project proposes the removal of eleven (11) existing on-site trees and the planting of ten (10) trees, consisting of 10 ground floor on-site trees. The three (3) Street Trees adjacent to the site were originally proposed for preservation subject to the discretion of the Urban Forestry Division. However, for purposes of conservative analysis and the requirements of CEQA, Planning has analyzed the worst-case potential for removal of all street trees. At the time of writing, the Urban Forestry Division has approved the removal of one (1) of the three (3) Street Trees. This environmental analysis does not authorize the removal of any street trees without prior approval of Urban Forestry, in compliance with LAMC Sections 62.169 and 62.170 and their applicable findings. Note, no Street Tree or protected tree may be removed without prior approval of the Board of Public Works/Urban Forestry (BPW) under LAMC Sections 62.161 - 62.171.

ceqa-3e80e597212ded0482.name: Viewpoint Amphitheater Project
ceqa-3e80e597212ded0482.description: Viewpoint School, a private TK–12 school, proposes construction and operation of a new outdoor amphitheater on its existing campus to expand the school’s performing arts and outdoor instructional facilities. The Viewpoint School campus occupies approximately 19 acres. The Project would not increase student enrollment or school capacity and would not result in an increase in the number of students or staff on campus. The amphitheater would serve as an alternate venue for existing school programs and events currently held in other on-campus facilities. The Project would involve demolition of an existing outdoor education area within the campus and development of a terraced hillside amphitheater. The amphitheater would include terraced hillside seating accommodating approximately 531 persons, including eight accessible seating spaces. The Project would also include construction of a performance bandshell with a structural truss system designed to support lighting and sound equipment, as well as a control booth to house audiovisual equipment. To improve campus circulation and accessibility, the Project would include construction of a new pedestrian bridge crossing Dry Canyon Creek, connecting the existing parking lot area and campus buildings to the amphitheater site. Additional pedestrian access would be provided via existing ramps from the Primary School and a proposed wooden walkway extending from the Academic Hall Terrace. The boardwalk would include an integrated outdoor classroom seating area as part of the boardwalk structure, located beneath existing sycamore trees to support outdoor instructional use. The school’s existing garden program would be relocated to a new area situated above the amphitheater. The relocated garden would include raised planting beds and a chicken coop, consistent with Viewpoint School’s commitment to sustainability and hands-on learning. Numerous coastal live oaks, willows, and landscaping trees are in this area.
ceqa-3e80e597212ded0482.crossStreets: Mulholland Highway and Old Topanga Canyon Road

ceqa-a5c76601381f5ae2c9.name: 834408_0100006_SoCalGas_UGS
ceqa-a5c76601381f5ae2c9.description: Southern California Gas Company proposes to Rework existing Gas Storage well Fernando Fee 32 at Aliso Canyon UGS 0100006. The intent of this project is to inspect the well integrity and remediate identified conditions as part of the Storage Integrity Management Program (SIMP). After reviewing well history, available directional surveys and inspection logs, and current wellbore configuration (casing size, restrictions, perforations, liner, etc.), a plan has been developed to return the well to service. This project includes pulling completion equipment, cleaning to total depth, performing punch and inject, and probable casing expansions as proposed and with approval from CalGEM, perform integrity tests, and run new completion tubing. Temporary equipment such as a mud pump and return bins will be utilized. No permanent facilities will be constructed during the process and no expansion of associated facilities will be required. All waste material, including brine kill fluid, will be properly disposed of as non-hazardous or hazardous waste, as appropriate, at a facility licensed to accept the waste. The established oil field surrounding the project location consists of graded pads, wells, oilfield equipment and roadways with areas of undisturbed non-native grasses and California sage brush vegetation. The proposed project consists of the California Department of Conservation, Geologic Energy Management Division (CalGEM) approving 1 permit for Southern California Gas Company (S4700) to rework the well listed below, in the Aliso Canyon Gas Field. API # Well Name 0403700686 Fernando Fee 32

ceqa-43e4de238519fe2115.name: Emergency Permit for Management of Hazardous Waste, City of Los Angeles, Department of General Services, Los Angeles, California
ceqa-43e4de238519fe2115.projectTitle: Emergency Permit for Management of Hazardous Waste, City of Los Angeles, Department of General Services, Los Angeles, California
ceqa-43e4de238519fe2115.agency: California Department of Toxic Substances Control
ceqa-43e4de238519fe2115.description: Project Description: The California Department of Toxic Substances Control (DTSC), pursuant to authority granted under California Code of Regulations (CCR), Title 22, Division 4.5, Chapter 20, Sec. 66270.61, has issued an Emergency Permit to City of Los Angeles, Department of General Services (EPA ID# CAD981576077) to treat hazardous waste through a controlled reaction with a chemical solution. Specifically, two (2) 1-liter containers of Diethyl Ether must be stabilized prior to transport to an authorized hazardous waste treatment, storage, and disposal facility. This chemical is currently being stored at the City of Los Angeles, Department of General Services located at 2319 Dorris Place, Los Angeles, California 90031. DTSC has determined as a safety precaution to prevent an accident or severe injury, an Emergency Permit should be issued to chemically stabilize the hazardous waste prior to storage and eventual transportation off-site. Background: The containers have peroxide formation present on either the inside, outside, or the bottom of the chemical’s containers, as well as the thread container caps. The presence of peroxide formation may be unstable at relatively low concentrations, resulting in fire and/or explosion if improperly handled. Due to the presence of peroxide formation, DTSC considers this chemical to be an imminent and substantial endangerment to human health and the environment. Chemical stabilization is recommended prior to transport to a permitted treatment, storage, and disposal facility. Project Activities: The treatment of these hazardous wastes involves the addition of a solution to the containers in a controlled manner to reduce the reactive or ignitable characteristics of the chemical. Treatment will take place within a designated exclusion zone. Only technicians from Clean Harbors will be allowed in the exclusion zone. Movement, preparation, and treatment of the containers will be in accordance with established standards. Within 10 business days of the expiration of this permit, the City of Los Angeles, Department of General Services will submit a final report, signed in accordance with Title 22, CCR Sec. 66270.11(d). The report shall include certification that the treatment area has been cleared of all residual hazardous waste generated from this emergency treatment and all generated waste has been properly managed. The Emergency Permit is effective beginning August 19, 2026 and shall expire on October 19, 2026.

The project will use signage, striping, plastic/rubber bollards, curbing, and other quick-build materials within the existing roadway; no physical construction is included. ceqa-ab890f57ccccf59ea8.name: Vineland Family Housing Removal Action Workplan
ceqa-ab890f57ccccf59ea8.projectTitle: Vineland Family Housing Removal Action Workplan
ceqa-ab890f57ccccf59ea8.agency: California Department of Toxic Substances Control
ceqa-ab890f57ccccf59ea8.description: The project consists of implementing a Removal Action Workplan (RAW) to address concentrations of volatile organic compounds (VOCs) in soil and sub-slab vapor on a 2.18 acre parcel located at 8015 and 8025 Vineland Avenue in Los Angeles, California (“Site”). The RAW proposes implementation of a vapor intrusion mitigation system (VIMS) with passive sub-slab ventilation (SSV) beneath two buildings that are proposed for development at the Site, along with adoption of a Land Use Covenant (LUC). Background: The Site is located in the Sun Valley neighborhood of Los Angeles and is identified as Los Angeles County Assessor’s Parcel Number (APN) 2314-006-002. The Site is an “L-shaped” parcel, roughly bounded on the west and northwest by apartments and residential properties, on the south by Strathern Street, on the east by Vineland Avenue, and on the north and southeast by commercial properties. The Site is currently vacant except for the concrete building foundation of a former 20,181-square-foot building, historically used as a grocery/market, which was destroyed in a fire in July 2021. Additionally, a temporary building and storage containers associated with a recycling center are located off Strathern Street in the southwest portion of the Site. The remaining portions of the Site consist of asphalt-paved parking areas and driveways providing access from Strathern Street to the south and Vineland Avenue to the east. DTSC and Las Palmas Housing and Development Corporation entered into a Voluntary Cleanup Agreement (Docket Number HSA-FY21/22-115 signed on March 29, 2022) to address contaminants on the Site. The Site is planned to be redeveloped with mixed-used commercial and multi-family/senior residential uses. Redevelopment of the Site entails the construction of a 6-story mixed-use building on the eastern/central portion of the Site (Vineland Apartments), which would include 136 affordable apartment dwelling units, 26,056 square feet of ground-floor commercial space, and underground parking. Additional development on the western portion (Strathern Senior Apartments) includes a 5-story building consisting of 97 affordable senior housing units, common areas, and underground parking. Two single-story underground parking structures are proposed to a depth of 12 feet beneath the majority of the Site apart from the southern portion of the senior development. Vehicular access to the Site is proposed at Vineland Avenue via two separate driveways and Strathern Street via one driveway, with reciprocal access at the northern adjacent property. It is noted that the City of Los Angeles previously determined that each of the land use development projects with which the subject RAW is associated are statutorily exempt from CEQA as a ministerial action pursuant to Public Resources Code Section 21080(b)(1) and Los Angeles Municipal Code (“LAMC”) Section 12.22 A.31. The City issued SB 35 Letters of Compliance dated April 20, 2023, to the RP regarding the ministerial approvals. The subject site mitigation and cleanup activities set forth in the RAW are considered discretionary approvals subject to CEQA and are outside the scope of the activities determined to be statutorily exempt. Previous Investigations: Investigations at the Site indicate that the primary Chemicals of Potential Concern (COPCs) include PCE, benzene, ethylbenzene, chloroform, dichlorodifluoromethane, and 1,2-DCA, which were detected at concentrations exceeding applicable screening levels (SLs). Per information provided in the RAW, soil investigation results did not indicate any COPCs in soil exceeding SLs, or potential on-Site sources of the reported soil vapor impacts. Groundwater is estimated to be at a depth of greater than 300 feet below ground surface (bgs). Based on the soil sampling results, soil and/or groundwater does not appear to have been potentially impacted by historical operations at the Site. Project Activities: The activities outlined in the RAW consist of implementing a VIMS with passive SSV beneath the two proposed buildings. The SSV system is designed for soil vapor to be passively diverted into the venting system and safely discharged to the atmosphere by means of vertical vent risers terminating at the building roof line. The venting system will consist of a sub-slab gravel layer beneath the entire footprint of the building that contains low-profile, 1-inch sub-slab collection pipes, which will transition to 3-inch rigid polyvinyl chloride pipe where penetration though building footers occurs. The collection pipes will be connected to carbon steel vertical risers along the building exterior that terminate above the roof line. An impervious membrane barrier will be installed above the sub-slab passive venting system and beneath the entire extent of the building footprint. The horizontal membrane barrier will consist of a minimum cured thickness of 60 mil (0.06 inches) Liquid Boot Plus VI-20 geomembrane. Monitoring probes will be placed within the gravel layer (below the membrane) and terminate in monitoring vaults outside the building perimeter wall. Sub-slab soil vapor monitoring probes will be used to monitor soil vapor concentrations under the slab. The VIMS installation will be implemented as part of the same construction activities which have already been approved for development through the City of Los Angeles’s SB 35 streamlined environmental review process. Installation of the VIMS would not require any substantial changes to the timing or duration of site preparation and construction activities, the type of equipment utilized as part of site preparation and construction, or the number of workers involved or number of worker transportation trips for the site preparation and construction processes. VIMS installation will not require any changes to the site boundaries, building footprint, aesthetic design, or operational characteristics from what was previously evaluated. In addition, a Land Use Covenant (LUC) will be recorded with Los Angeles County to ensure notifications are made to DTSC prior to any future earthwork activities at the Site, prevent disturbance of the vapor barrier, and ensure the prohibition of any groundwater extraction. Although not anticipated, in the event biological, cultural or historical resources are discovered in the course of project activities, work will be suspended while a qualified biologist, cultural or historical specialist makes an assessment of the area and arrangements are made to protect or preserve any resources that are discovered. If human remains are discovered, no further disturbance will occur in the location where the remains are found, and the County Coroner will be notified pursuant to the Health and Safety Code, Chapter 2, Section 7050.5.

ceqa-c1dcb9516897d086b7.name: Additional Measures in the Proposed Addendum to the Cooperative Agreement between South Coast AQMD and the Ports of Long Beach and Los Angeles
ceqa-c1dcb9516897d086b7.projectTitle: Proposed Amended Rule (PAR) 1111 – Reduction of NOx Emissions from Natural Gas-Fired Furnaces, (continued)
ceqa-c1dcb9516897d086b7.agency: South Coast Air Quality Management District
ceqa-c1dcb9516897d086b7.agencyName: South Coast Air Quality Management District
ceqa-c1dcb9516897d086b7.description: A Cooperative Agreement between South Coast AQMD and Ports of Long Beach and Los Angeles (Cooperative Agreement), which was approved by the South Coast AQMD Governing Board on November 7, 2025, and executed on December 17, 2025, requires the Ports to develop and implement charging and fueling infrastructure plans. The proposed Addendum to the Cooperative Agreement has been subsequently developed which: 1) includes three additional measures requiring the Ports to enhance their current clean ship incentive programs to encourage port calls from the cleanest ocean-going vessels, to develop and implement a new incentive program to encourage utilization of zero-emission trucks, and to allocate funds to South Coast AQMD for regional off-port zero-emission truck charging and fueling infrastructure projects; 2) incorporates a provision for South Coast AQMD to recover reasonable costs for newly introduced staff expenses; and 3) directs payment for contract defaults to go into the Clean Air Mitigation Fund previously established in the Cooperative Agreement. The cost recovery provision in the Proposed Addendum to the Cooperative Agreement, which was crafted to ensure that South Coast AQMD recovers the reasonable costs associated with the implementation and compliance activities, is statutorily exempt from CEQA and is not the focus of this Notice of Determination. A Notice of Exemption for the cost recovery provision has been filed and posted separately. Lastly, the direction requiring payments resulting from contractual defaults associated with the additional measures to be deposited into the existing Clean Air Mitigation Fund is not a project as defined by CEQA, does not change the prior determination that the creation of the Clean Air Mitigation Fund in the Cooperative Agreement is not considered a project within the meaning of CEQA, and is also not the focus of this Notice of Determination.

ceqa-018f7864af6c9b5d9d.name: Cooperative Agreement Addendum Between the Ports of Long Beach and Los Angeles, and the South Coast Air Quality Management District
ceqa-018f7864af6c9b5d9d.projectTitle: Cooperative Agreement Between the Ports of Long Beach and Los Angeles and the South Coast Air Quality Management District
ceqa-018f7864af6c9b5d9d.description: The Cooperative Agreement between the South Coast Air Quality Management District (AQMD), Port of Los Angeles, and Port of Long Beach was signed and executed by the parties in December 2025 and is effective through December 31, 2030. The Cooperative Agreement sets forth the requirements for implementation of Clean Air Action Plan (CAAP) Plus Measures through a three-phase process and schedule for the preparation and completion of zero-emission infrastructure plans for cargo-handling equipment, switcher locomotives, drayage trucks, and ocean-going vessels, with provisions for transparency and accountability with enforcement penalties if the ports do not adhere to the identified schedules and requirements. The Cooperative Agreement Addendum adds new CAAP Plus measures to provide incentives for the use of cleaner ocean-going vessels and drayage trucks and a mechanism to fund regional off-port truck charging and fueling infrastructure. Development of the Enhanced Clean Ship Incentive Program would enhance the existing Green Ship Incentive Program to increase program participation with potential CAAP “plus-up” incentives for the cleanest vessels, involving collection of information regarding the description of ocean-going vessels that typically call at the port, annual visits by vessel type, engine tier level and fuel type, current participation levels, and a comparison of vessels that participate in the current Green Ship Incentive Program, and those that do not participate by vessel type, engine tier, and fuel type, as well as the participation goals anticipated for the Enhanced Clean Ship Incentive Program based on available information known at the time of the program’s development. The program is to be approved no later than 12 months after approval of the update to the International Association of Ports and Harbors Environmental Ship Index Program. Each port would evaluate and develop a Zero-Emission Truck Utilization Incentive Program to be funded by the Port’s established Clean Truck Fund Rate to encourage the use of zero-emission trucks serving the ports involving development of the general guidelines, incentive amounts, and mechanism of providing the incentive to participating truck fleets, with justification for the incentive approach describing the consideration and factors taken into account to develop the program concept, which may include port policies and goals, findings from technical studies, stakeholder outreach, software and hardware requirements, and operational and financial considerations. The program shall also include anticipated participation goals, based on the available information known at the time of concept development; justification for the participation goals (with understanding that the participation goals are outside the control of the ports); anticipated program benefits; and metrics for tracking and reporting of clean air benefits. The Zero-Emission Truck Utilization Incentive Program is to be approved no later than February 28, 2027. The details and anticipated cost for the Enhanced Clean Ships Incentive Program and Zero-Emission Truck Utilization Incentive will be defined through a public process and considered for approval by the Board of Harbor Commissioners. The Regional Off-Port Truck Charging and Fueling Infrastructure CAAP Plus Measure would allocate $20 million to the South Coast AQMD to fund development of zero-emission infrastructure for drayage trucks outside of the ports. A memorandum of understanding to transfer the funds is required to be approved and entered into no later than February 28, 2027. The Cooperative Agreement Addendum also defines the South Coast AQMD’s role, the ports’ commitment to a public process, involving release of draft materials for a period of at least 45 days for review and comment by the South Coast AQMD, one public meeting to highlight key elements of the draft, and preparation of written responses to all comments received. If a port defaults on the terms of the Cooperative Agreement Addendum by missing a deadline or failing to adhere to the public process, the port will be subject to payment into a Clean Air Mitigation Fund in the amount of $50,000 and up to $100,000, depending on the nature of the default. The Clean Air Mitigation Fund will be managed by the South Coast AQMD for disbursement to projects within the Tidelands Trust area. The Cooperative Agreement Addendum also requires annual reporting by the ports on progress of the incentive and funding programs during the 5-year term of the agreement. To support emissions reductions from port operations, the preamble to the Cooperative Agreement Addendum identifies the concurrent activities that the ports will conduct through a public process through the term of the original Cooperative Agreement. These activities would consist of the development and implementation of a clean marine fuel assessment, a solicitation for a clean marine fuel pilot project, a technical study on vessel emissions at low-speed operations, preparation of a clean truck rate spending plan, and projection for zero-emission cargo-handling equipment deployments.

ceqa-95328ae8e295c1c33d.name: Gindi Maimonides Academy Campus Improvements Project
ceqa-95328ae8e295c1c33d.projectTitle: Gindi Maimonides Academy Campus Improvements Project
ceqa-95328ae8e295c1c33d.description: The Gindi Maimonides Academy (GMA) is a private school located in the City of West Hollywood and City of Los Angeles. The proposed project would improve the portion of the GMA campus located within West Hollywood (“project site”). The project would involve demolishing all existing improvements on the project site, totaling 16,000 square feet of building demolition and demolition of approximately 45,000 square feet of surface parking and outdoor recreational area removals. The project site would be redeveloped with a 3-story, 41,000–square foot educational building and a 2-story, 12,000–square foot indoor gymnasium. The new educational building would include a new cafeteria, classrooms, faculty and administrative rooms, and spaces for kindergarten, second-year, daycare, nursery, pre-nursery, and parent/caregiver and child programming. Both buildings would be constructed over single-level subterranean parking garages, providing a total of approximately 88 parking spaces. The project would include establishing a specific plan for the project site, as well as expanding the enrollment capacity on the project site by 146 students, for a new total of 466 students.

ceqa-8db34e48ba32b26cf8.name: Sidewalk Repair Program
ceqa-8db34e48ba32b26cf8.projectTitle: City of Los Angeles Sidewalk Repair Program (Project)
ceqa-8db34e48ba32b26cf8.description: The Sidewalk Repair Program (the Project) is implemented citywide, over an area that covers approximately 467 square miles. The Project is a citywide program intended to modify the manner in which sidewalk repair projects are undertaken pursuant to the City's obligations under the Willits Settlement, which includes various City actions that will provide improved access to persons with mobility disabilities in accordance with local, state, and federal accessibility requirements. The Project includes an ordinance that will guide the construction of future sidewalk repairs; curb ramp repairs; crosswalk paving; street tree retention, removal and replacement; canopy pruning; root pruning; and applicable utility work for 30 years within the City. The new ordinance (LAMC 62.104.1) revises the way sidewalk repairs pursuant to the Willits Settlement, are reviewed and approved, and is intended generally to improve and streamline the implementation process. The primary components of the ordinance include: • Specific parameters to enable most sidewalk repairs to proceed as ministerial approvals, not subject to further environmental review applicable to discretionary actions. • A streamlined discretionary approval process for sidewalk repair projects falling ou1side the specific parameters allowed for a ministerial sidewalk repair approval. • A streamlined discretionary approval process for sidewalk repair projects involving the proposed removal of three or more street trees. • A revised Street Tree Retention, Removal and Replacement Policy. • Mandatory Project Design Features (PDFs) generally consisting of regulatory compliance measures and standard construction conditions and procedures.
