ceqa-22e3117fcbdb48fcea.name: Glencore Recycling LLC, Hazardous Waste Facility Permit Renewal
ceqa-22e3117fcbdb48fcea.projectTitle: Glencore Recycling LLC, Hazardous Waste Facility Permit Renewal
ceqa-22e3117fcbdb48fcea.agency: California Department of Toxic Substances Control
ceqa-22e3117fcbdb48fcea.description: The California Department of Toxic Substances Control (DTSC), pursuant to authority granted under California Code of Regulations, Title 22, Division 4.5, Chapter 20 has issued a Standardized Series B Hazardous Waste Facility Permit Renewal (Permit Renewal) for Glencore Recycling LLC (Facility) for ten additional years. This Permit Renewal will allow the Facility to continue to treat and store liquid and solid hazardous waste at the Facility. This Permit Renewal includes the addition of two new miscellaneous units for triple washing containers, and a reduction in the overall volume of hazardous waste the Facility is permitted to treat. The Facility Permit will change from a Series A to Series B Standardized Permit. Pursuant to Health and Safety Code section 25143, DTSC is also granting a variance to the Permittee conditionally exempting Unit 1, Unit 2, and Unit 7a from the setback requirement specified in California Code of Regulations, title 22, section 66264.176.There are no other proposed changes and no physical changes that require construction and/or ground disturbance for the Permit Renewal. Background: The site of the Facility has been used for heavy manufacturing operations since the 1930s. Metal recycling operations were established at this location in the early 1970s and underwent many different names before settling with Glencore Recycling LLC in 2015. The Facility area is approximately 2.2 acres in a developed industrial area. DTSC initially issued a Permit to the Facility on November 1, 1994, and renewed the Permit on May 6, 2012. The Facility area is composed of a warehouse, offices, and treatment and storage areas that are used to process different materials for metals recovery including electronic scraps, components, manufacturing byproducts, wastes, concentrates, and residues. Project Activities: The Facility generates and receives precious metal bearing acid solutions that are stored in designated areas before and after treatment. Treatment of acid solutions includes pH adjustment, precipitation, neutralization, and/or evaporation to convert precious metals into solid form. Tray furnaces are used to bake solids containing combustible organics, dry inorganic sludge, and to evaporate water from neutral and alkaline solutions. Hazardous waste solids, sludge, scrap metal, and excluded recyclable materials are melted in crucible furnaces to recover, refine, or separate metals. Mechanical processing such as grinding, milling, screening, and blending of ash, sludge, and other solids in miscellaneous units to prepare and collect a representative sample of metals for analysis to facilitate further recovery operations. Dry and wet additives may be combined with treated material to improve handling and flow properties. The Permit will authorize the Facility to operate 12 existing hazardous waste management units (HWMU) and install two new miscellaneous units for triple washing containers. The Facility will be authorized to store up to a maximum of 3,300 gallons of liquid hazardous waste and 153 tons of solid hazardous waste, and treat 50,000 gallons per month of liquid hazardous waste and 50 tons per month of solid hazardous waste. The addition of the two miscellaneous units will not require any construction or ground disturbance. The Permit will also authorize a variance from the setback requirement specified in California Code of Regulations, title 22, section 66264.176 for Units 1, 2, and 7a. The variance will not cause any operational changes as containers within these units are currently and will continue to be within 50 feet of the property line. There are no other proposed changes to the Facility, or any of the waste being stored or treated, or to any other operations or units. There will be no operational changes or ground disturbance. All previous Permit requirements will remain in effect. This Permit Renewal will not result in any new or substantially more severe significant impacts on the environment.

ceqa-e526a2ecb2e32b60f7.name: Approval of Local Energy Efficiency and Conservation Standards Application Findings Submitted by the City of Sunnyvale for the 2022 Energy Code Cycle
ceqa-e526a2ecb2e32b60f7.projectTitle: Approval of Local Energy Efficiency and Conservation Standards Application Findings Submitted by the City of Sunnyvale for the 2022 Energy Code Cycle
ceqa-e526a2ecb2e32b60f7.description: The California Energy Commission (CEC) adopts and regularly updates regulations that define a process for local governments to apply to the CEC to make certain findings regarding locally adopted energy conservation or energy insulation standards (CCR, Title 24, Part 1, section 10-106 and section 10-110; Public Resources Code section 25402.1(h)(2)). The local government’s proposed standards are often referred to as the Local Reach Codes and require local governments submit an application to the CEC consistent with the requirements listed in section 10-106(b). Before the local standards may be enforced, the CEC must make two non-discretionary findings pursuant to PRC section 25402.1(h)(2) and as listed in section 10-106(a): 1) The proposed local standards will require the diminution of energy consumption levels compared to the 2022 Energy Code, and 2) The local government has filed the basis of its cost-effectiveness determination with the CEC. On September 04, 2025, the City of Sunnyvale (the City) submitted an application to the CEC that included: 1) the basis of its determination that the locally adopted energy efficiency standards contained in Ordinance No. 3244-25 are cost-effective; and (2) documentation that the locally adopted energy efficiency standards contained in Ordinance No. 3244-25 will require the diminution of energy consumption levels compared to the 2022 Building Energy Efficiency Standards (Energy Code), as required by PRC section 25402.1(h)(2) and by CCR, Title 24, Part 1, section 10-106 (section 10-106). Based on the information submitted, staff analysis, and the Executive Director's recommendation, the CEC approved findings of the City’s section 10-106 application at the CEC’s November 12, 2025, Business Meeting.

ceqa-bf8c08886a7cd1b7f3.projectTitle: 749 West El Camino Real Mixed-Use Project
ceqa-bf8c08886a7cd1b7f3.description: The project would demolish the existing 1,487 square foot restaurant building, 18,302 square foot bank building, and all associated surface parking and landscaping on-site to construct two new buildings on-site: 1) a two-story, 8,483 square foot bank building and 2) a six-story mixed-use building with 299 multi-family residential units (31 units of which would be reserved for very-low- income and two units for low-income households), 10,830 square feet of ground-floor commercial uses, and at-grade podium parking above two levels of underground parking. The new bank would be located on the northwest corner of the project site and a public plaza is proposed on El Camino Real between the proposed bank building and mixed-use building’s ground-floor commercial uses. The project would preserve the existing artwork pieces associated with the existing bank building and plaza and incorporate them into the new development. Implementation of the project would require the removal of existing trees, including Heritage Trees. The proposed project would plant replacement trees in conformance with City requirements. The project also includes utility and right-of-way improvements. The project would meet Tier 1 development standards per the El Camino Real Precise Plan and have a maximum structure height of 6 stories (or 75 feet) and a floor-area-ratio (FAR) of approximately 3.05 (98 dwelling units per acre [du/ac]). The project would utilize State Density Bonus Law to exceed the allowed zoning density of 2.3 FAR with a 46.25 percent density bonus, as calculated based on Mountain View’s Density Bonus Program Guidelines and Section 36.48.75 (General Provisions for Density Bonus) of the City Code. The project does not require a General Plan amendment or rezoning. The project approval included a Planned Community Permit, Development Review Permit, Provisional Use Permit, Heritage Tree Removal Permit, and a resolution for the vacation of public easements at the project site.

ceqa-7f0a8d72c2f5180841.name: 901 N.Rengstorff Avenue Project (project addresses includes 901-987 N.Rengstorff)
ceqa-7f0a8d72c2f5180841.projectTitle: 901 N.Rengstorff Avenue Project (project addresses includes 901-987 N.Rengstorff)
ceqa-7f0a8d72c2f5180841.description: 901 North Rengstorff Avenue Project Project Description – November 2025 The Project Applicant, Mario Ambra, proposes the 901 North Rengstorff Avenue Project (Project), which involves demolition of all existing structures and development of a multi-family residential building on an approximately 1.26-acre (54,782 square-foot) Project site located at 901, 913 and 987 N. Rengstorff Avenue in the City of Mountain View. The project site is located on the east side of N. Rengstorff Avenue between Leghorn Street and Plymouth Street, just south of the U.S. 101 Highway, and is bounded by N. Rengstorff Avenue to the west, a former olive oil factory currently used as a single-family home to the north, existing residential/commercial uses to the east, and Plymouth Street to the south. The Project site contains an approximately 2,253-square-foot multi-family residential building at the southwest corner of the Project site, three accessory buildings at the southeastern portion of the Project site, and an accessory building toward the northern boundary of the Project site. The Project is proposed as a “Builder's Remedy” housing development under the Builder’s Remedy provisions of the Housing Accountability Act (Gov. Code §65589.5). The Project would demolish all existing structures on the Project site and construct an approximately 499,525-square-foot, 15-story multi-family residential building. The proposed building would contain 455 residential units (20% affordable) comprised of 183 studios, 142 one-bedroom units and 130 two-bedroom units. Additionally, the Project would include approximately 15,818 square feet of common open space and 1,313 square feet of private open space. The maximum building height would be approximately 184 feet. The Project would provide 429 garage parking spaces and 356 bicycle parking spaces. Vehicular access to the Project site would be provided via a new 24-foot parking garage entrance on the southern border of the Project site along Plymouth Street. The Project building would connect to existing City infrastructure in N. Rengstorff Avenue and Plymouth Street. The Project would remove 67 on site trees, consisting of 19 Heritage Trees and 48 non-heritage trees. The Project would plant a total of 52 replacement trees. In addition, the Project would relocate 5 Olive trees (4 Heritage) to the northwest corner of 987 N. Rengstorff Avenue immediately adjacent to the former olive oil facility. The project request includes development permits (“Entitlements”) required by the City of Mountain View to construct the building and a Lot Line Adjustment to create the project site and the parcel to the north (for the olive oil factory). Project construction would be developed in a single phase and is anticipated to last up to 30 months beginning in April 2028 and ending by October 2030. The City of Mountain View prepared an AB 130 consistency analysis for the Project that determined the Project meets the criteria for a CEQA exempt housing project under AB 130, including the environmental factors under Public Resources Code Section 21080.66, and the Project is eligible to use the statutory exemption under AB 130. This document is available for review from the City of Mountain View upon request. The City of Mountain View City Council approved the Project, including the above-noted CEQA exemption, on November 18, 2025.

ceqa-9e4d0d50322ba027bd.name: California Avenue Two-Lot Subdivision

Future improvements would also include the construction of a shared well on Parcel 1, and septic system and fire protection improvements on each parcel. No tree removal is proposed. Once the property is subdivided, Parcel 1 and Parcel 2 could each be developed with a single-family residence, an accessory dwelling unit, and a junior accessory dwelling unit. Future home development would be served by a shared well and individual onsite septic systems. No construction of residences is proposed as part of this subdivision.

ceqa-b3e874df475c0b2430.name: Al Shugart Dog Park
ceqa-b3e874df475c0b2430.description: The Al Shugart Dog Park ("project") is being proposed by the City of Scotts Valley to develop a dog park with additional park amenities. The project site is located on two partially-developed parcels (APNs 023-241-21 and -22) and one undeveloped parcel (023-241-11) at 400 Glenwood Drive in the City of Scotts Valley, Santa Cruz County. Improvements are proposed on approximately 5.64 acres of the property (“project site”). The project site consists of vacant open space and a small parking lot located in the southwest corner of the project site. The City proposes to develop a dog park with additional park amenities. The project would include improvements such as pet-proof fencing and dog park entry corrals; landscaping and irrigation. Pathway lighting along the existing multi-use pathway connecting to the project site and security lighting at the restroom is proposed. Park-user amenities would include the following: a 6,500 square-foot all-weather turf area; 9,000 square-foot area for small dogs; 28,000 square-foot area for large dogs; prefabricated restroom structure with two single use ADA-compliant stalls; park dedication monument; walking paths; benches, picnic areas, and seating areas; metal shade features; outdoor classroom; bike racks; drinking fountains; and, trash and recycling receptacles. The proposed project would require water service for drinking fountains, the restroom, and landscaping, and would connect to existing Scotts Valley Water District water service infrastructure near the project site. The proposed project would require lateral connections and routing to the City’s existing wastewater collection system, and would construct biotreatment planters for stormwater treatment and infiltration. The proposed project would involve the repair of an existing parking lot on Glenwood Road and parking lot expansion, resulting in a total of up to 42 spaces. The project site currently consists of vacant open space and a small parking lot located in the southwest corner of the project site.
ceqa-b3e874df475c0b2430.developmentType: Recreational (Dog park, and repair and expansion of an existing parking lot.)

ceqa-2dc8d892c049c94f23.name: 810 3rd Street Site Improvements
ceqa-2dc8d892c049c94f23.description: The project consists of a Coastal Permit, Administrative Use Permit, and Design Permit to modify an existing parking lot to provide a total of 25 parking spaces, to construct a laundry room addition, conduct utility trenching, and to install a fence on a property with an existing motel use within the boundaries of the Beach South of Laurel Area Plan. The site contains known archaeological resources.

ceqa-68fd3c89a85edf0ea5.name: Wastewater Energy and Electrical Resiliency Project
ceqa-68fd3c89a85edf0ea5.projectTitle: Wastewater Energy and Electrical Resiliency Project
ceqa-68fd3c89a85edf0ea5.description: The Wastewater Energy and Electrical Resiliency (WEER) Project would modernize and replace aging electrical infrastructure at the City Wastewater Treatment Facility (WWTF) to improve electrical system reliability, resiliency, operational flexibility, worker safety, and emergency preparedness. Most of the electrical distribution systems at the facility were installed in the 1980’s and 1990’s. While well maintained, it has exceeded its useful life and creates operational and maintenance challenges. The project includes replacement of deteriorated underground electrical distribution lines, completion of a redundant facility-wide electrical loop, replacement and consolidation of substations, transformers, and switchgear, construction of a new main electrical building, demolition of the existing maintenance building, installation of a new centralized standby power generation system, and upgrades to electrical equipment serving treatment processes such as interstage pumps and aeration blowers. The project would also replace obsolete medium-voltage equipment with modern electrical systems, incorporate upgraded controls and variable-frequency drives to improve operational efficiency, and provide infrastructure capable of supporting long-term WWTF operations. Replacements and upgrades are needed to improve reliability, safety, maintainability, and alignment with current standards to establish a 30-to-40-year service lifespan.

ceqa-38d7c18e0fe32c419f.name: Cunnison Lane Well Outfall Addendum
ceqa-38d7c18e0fe32c419f.projectTitle: Soquel Creek Water District Well Master Plan
ceqa-38d7c18e0fe32c419f.description: The Soquel Creek Water District proposes modifications to the Well Master Plan Environmental Impact Report to move the Cunnison Lane Well Site outfall from its proposed location to an adjacent unnamed tributary. The Modified Project would involve installing an underground pipeline, an outfall, and an energy dissipation system.

ceqa-3ee59d0f5c3b319d4e.name: New Brighton Middle School Modernization and District Facilities Project
ceqa-3ee59d0f5c3b319d4e.projectTitle: New Brighton Middle School Modernization and District Facilities Project
ceqa-3ee59d0f5c3b319d4e.description: The project scope for Phase I of the modernization at New Brighton Middle School broadly includes the following: renovation of Admin/Student Services Building E including new floor finishes, new casework, new exterior door installation, and minor power and data upgrades; flooring replacement in Room 38 of Classroom Building F; modernization of Buildings K (classrooms), L (classrooms) and M (Library), including new finishes, casework, minor door/window replacement, new exterior awnings, minor structural modifications, plumbing and mechanical upgrades, and electrical (power, data, lighting and fire alarm) upgrades; renovation of Gymnasium Building P, including restroom upgrades (including finishes and plumbing fixtures), backstop replacement (with related structural upgrades), new exterior awnings and minor power, data and lighting upgrades; and site improvements include accessibility upgrades, paving removal and replacement, minor landscaping/irrigation/storm drain and fencing scope. The project scope for Phase II of the modernization broadly includes the following: Classroom modernization of Buildings D, E and F, including new flooring, patch repair and painting of existing wall and ceiling surfaces, new casework and modifications to existing casework to remain, door/window replacement (including window curtain removal), new exterior awnings, minor structural modifications, plumbing upgrades (at classroom sink location), and electrical (power and data) upgrades and bracing of existing light fixtures. Exterior classroom scope to include removal of existing lockers and related exterior finish wall surface repair; modernization of Special Ed Admin Building H to include finish and electrical upgrades (interior doors to remain) and reconfiguration of existing restrooms into gender-neutral, ADA compliant restrooms; restroom (single occupancy and multiple- accommodation) modernization of Buildings D, E and F, including partial removal of finishes at walls, floor and ceiling to stud and related patch/repair/painting of those surfaces. Restroom scope to also include toilet partition replacement and selective plumbing fixture replacement; refinishing of existing MP wood stage flooring; site improvements include accessibility upgrades, paving removal and replacement, landscaping/irrigation/storm drain improvements (primarily in classroom courtyards), two new shade structures, renovation of covered walkway roofs including stucco soffit replacement, replacement of existing roofing (including flashing and gutters) and abandonment/removal of obsolete roof-mounted utilities and a campus-wide fire alarm upgrade. The project also includes a District Office and MOT Department facility component, which broadly includes the following: Renovations/tenant improvements to the existing District Office building including reconfiguration of interior rooms/spaces (with new interior partitions), new interior finishes, exterior wall finishes/roofing improvements, door and window replacement, new casework, new restrooms and utility improvements including power, signal/LV (including lighting and fire alarm), mechanical and plumbing upgrades. Demolition of the existing Board Room/tech offices portable building and replacement with a new pre-engineered Steel Building facility that may include a bus/maintenance shop, offices, restrooms, and storage rooms. Site improvements to include site DWK 4343130v1 paving and landscaping improvements, site security (fencing/gates) and pertinent underground utility (dry and wet) upgrades.

ceqa-073773edcf004c65fe.name: Soquel Elementary School Modernization Project Phases I and II
ceqa-073773edcf004c65fe.projectTitle: Soquel Elementary School Modernization Project Phases I and II
ceqa-073773edcf004c65fe.description: The project scope for Phase I of the modernization at Soquel Elementary School is the DSA review and approval phase and broadly includes the following: Modernization of Building 1A (Administration/Library/Classrooms), including new interior partitions, finishes, casework, doors/windows (including replacement of existing), restroom upgrades, structural modifications, plumbing and mechanical upgrades, and electrical (power, data, signal, lighting and fire alarm) upgrades. Site improvements include accessibility upgrades, paving removal and replacement, and minor storm drain scope. The project scope for Phase II of the modernization is the schematic design phase and broadly includes the following: Modernization of four classrooms (Kindergarten/TKK) in Buildings 2 and 3, including new finishes, casework, door replacement, electrical upgrades (power/data/signal/lighting) and mechanical upgrades. Modernization of two existing restrooms and provision of four new restrooms in Buildings 2 and 3. Two of the new restrooms will include exterior wall/ceiling framing, finishes, doors, MEP, etc. Modernization of the existing MP room and minor modernization of the existing kitchen. Site improvements include accessibility upgrades, AC paving removal and replacement in the Kindergarten/TKK Classroom Buildings 2 and 3 courtyard (and related storm drain system adjustments), new shade structure in the same courtyard, landscaping and irrigation improvements in the two planter/landscaped areas at the school frontage and campus-wide fire alarm upgrade.

ceqa-3b2e9b89a6a82c65da.name: Capitola Road at Leona Creek Culvert Rehabilitation Project (Notification of Streambed Alteration, No. EPIMS-SCR-62645-R3)
ceqa-3b2e9b89a6a82c65da.projectTitle: Capitola Road at Leona Creek Culvert Rehabilitation Project (Notification of Streambed Alteration, No. EPIMS-SCR-62645-R3)
ceqa-3b2e9b89a6a82c65da.agency: California Department of Fish and Wildlife, Bay Delta Region 3
ceqa-3b2e9b89a6a82c65da.agencyName: Fish and Wildlife, Region 3 - Bay Delta, Fairfield
ceqa-3b2e9b89a6a82c65da.description: The California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) has executed Streambed Alteration Agreement EPIMS Notification No. EPIMS-SCR-62645-R3, pursuant to Section 1602 of the Fish and Game Code to Santa Cruz County - Flood Control and Water Conservation District. The Project is limited to rehabilitating 100 linear feet of an existing 66-inch diameter corrugated metal culvert pipe located below Capitola Road on private property within drainage easements. Temporary diversion dams composed of clean gravel and visqueen sheeting will be installed at 20 and 25 feet from the upstream and downstream ends of the culvert to isolate the work area. Once isolated, the culvert interior will be cleaned, voids will be filled with repair mortar, exterior voids will be compaction grouted with polyurethane geotechnical foam, and fiber-reinforced grout layers will be applied using a centrifugally cast concrete pipe machine. No grading and earthwork will occur, and access to the creek and bank will be limited to foot traffic for diversion dam and pump installation and removal. All work will be conducted through existing manholes with construction staging adjacent to the roadway.

ceqa-d00cacdf9dc3fd48a3.name: San Lorenzo Valley Water District Highland Tank Replacement Project
ceqa-d00cacdf9dc3fd48a3.projectTitle: San Lorenzo Valley Water District Highland Tank Replacement Project

ceqa-13a86eb44da0833423.name: Groundwater Sustainability Plan Periodic Review - Santa Cruz Mid-County Basin - October 2026
ceqa-13a86eb44da0833423.projectTitle: Groundwater Sustainability Plan Periodic Review - Santa Cruz Mid-County Basin - October 2026
ceqa-13a86eb44da0833423.description: The Sustainable Groundwater Management Act (SGMA), Water Code 10720 et seq., requires local groundwater sustainability agencies (GSAs) to develop and implement groundwater sustainability plans (GSPs). (Water Code 10727) The Department of Water Resources (DWR) is required to evaluate whether GSPs and their local implementation comply with certain provisions of SGMA, are likely to achieve sustainability, and whether they adversely affect the ability of adjacent basins to implement their GSPs. (Water Code 10733) DWR is required to issue an assessment within two years of submission of a GSP and again at least every five years during GSP implementation. (Water Code 10733.4, 10733.8) Accordingly, DWR conducted a 5-year periodic review of the Santa Cruz Mid-County Basin GSP and has issued an assessment that determines the GSP or its implementation is "approved." (23 Cal. Code Regs. 355.2, 355.6)

ceqa-723271642c0356bf63.name: Natural Bridges Monarch Grove Fuels Reduction
ceqa-723271642c0356bf63.projectTitle: Natural Bridges Monarch Grove Fuels Reduction
ceqa-723271642c0356bf63.agency: California Department of Parks and Recreation
ceqa-723271642c0356bf63.description: Project consists of fuels reduction at Natural Bridges State Beach for the purpose of enhancing monarch overwintering habitat. Work will take place prior to the overwintering season and will consist of using chainsaws to consolidate downed materials and accumulating ladder fuels into approximately 20 burn piles within the Monarch Butterfly Nature Preserve. Pile burning will occur April-May 2027 when conditions are favorable for prescription burning and after all monarchs have migrated away from the overwintering site.

ceqa-a5d518e3e1f618ab92.name: Natural Bridges Boardwalk Accessibility Improvements
ceqa-a5d518e3e1f618ab92.agency: California Department of Parks and Recreation
ceqa-a5d518e3e1f618ab92.description: Project proposes replacing the existing Monarch Butterfly Boardwalk at Natural Bridges State Beach for accessibility improvements. Work will: •Improve the paved access route from the visitor center to the boardwalk trailhead; •Install new concrete and asphalt walkways with truncated domes that connect to the existing accessible parking stalls in the main parking lot; •Remove the existing boardwalk and observation platform and utilize existing concrete pier foundations, and install new diamond piers to construct a new elevated boardwalk, with proper grades, clearances and safety rail configurations, that descends to the pond area; and •Remove and replace the bench seating along a portion of the boardwalk and observation platform.

ceqa-f9e4f57ace67df0a52.name: Application 251276 - Mission Drive Subdivision and Planned Unit Development (PUD)
ceqa-f9e4f57ace67df0a52.projectTitle: Application 251276 - Mission Drive Subdivision and Planned Unit Development (PUD)
ceqa-f9e4f57ace67df0a52.description: Proposal for a Subdivision and Planned Unit Development (PUD) to divide three parcels (APNs 025-032-33, 025-032-34, 025-032-35) to create six fee-simple lots with detached single-family dwellings. Five lots and a private street will be developed with access from Thurber Lane, and a sixth corridor access lot will be developed with access from Mission Drive. Project requires adoption of a PUD ordinance by the Board of Supervisors, Administrative Site Development Permit (ASP), a Subdivision Map, a preliminary grading review, and a soils report review.

ceqa-dfadd6c9b3599821d7.name: Atkinson Lane Integrated Flood Management and Watershed Restoration Project - Phase II – Stormwater BMP Bioswale and Wetland Enhancement
ceqa-dfadd6c9b3599821d7.projectTitle: Atkinson Lane Integrated Flood Management and Watershed Restoration Project - Phase II – Stormwater BMP Bioswale and Wetland Enhancement
ceqa-dfadd6c9b3599821d7.description: The proposed project includes construction of a vegetated bioswale and wetland retention basin and revegetation with native plants. The bioswale has been designed to improve water quality within the existing Atkinson Wetland Complex through stormwater capture and infiltration while also providing flood-risk reduction by enhancing the ability of the wetland complex to attenuate floods. The bioswale will tie into the City’s storm drain system at the outfall of an existing 18” storm drain pipe. Work will involve grading to create the new swale and retention basin, revegetation with native wetland and riparian plants, and installation of erosion control. Phase II construction will be implemented in collaboration with the Phase I Habitat Enhancement. All temporarily impacted areas will be restored with native plants upon project completion. Protective measures including worker training, surveys prior to work commencement, and daily monitoring will be implemented to ensure that project activities will not result in adverse impacts on any native wildlife species or their habitats.

ceqa-af1db2736b25be07a9.name: Watsonville General Plan 2050
ceqa-af1db2736b25be07a9.description: The Watsonville General Plan 2050 is a comprehensive update of the Watsonville 2005 General Plan to guide land use, mobility, housing, conservation, safety, public facilities, and other policy decisions through 2050. General Plan 2050 establishes a long-term community vision and planning framework for public and private development while responding to changed conditions and new State requirements including AB 1358 (Complete Streets), SB 99 (Evacuation Analysis), SB 379 (Climate Adaptation), SB 932 (Safe Systems), SB 1241 (Wildfire Hazards), and SB 1000 (Environmental Justice). General Plan 2050 focuses growth within Downtown Watsonville, along the Freedom Boulevard and East Lake Avenue corridors, and in identified new growth areas. It introduces a broader range of housing choices; supports new employment, commercial, regional retail, visitor-serving, and community recreation uses; preserves natural open space and agricultural resources; improves parks and community facilities; implements complete streets improvements; and supports rerouting truck traffic around the City. The plan would also update the City’s land use map, goals, policies, and implementation actions and would serve as a first-tier program-level planning document for future development. The full buildout projections for General Plan 2050 facilitate up to 5,980 new residential units and approximately 2.672 million square feet of nonresidential development. This includes approximately 4,560 residential units within the existing City limits; 1,420 residential units in the Area A (Buena Vista), Area B (Atkinson Lane) and/or Area C growth areas; 513,000 square feet of nonresidential development within the existing City limits; 2.129 million square feet of nonresidential development in the Highway 1 Gateway growth area; and 30,000 square feet of neighborhood-serving retail in the Buena Vista and Area C growth areas.
ceqa-af1db2736b25be07a9.developmentType: Other (5,980 residential units; 2.672 million sqft nonresidential space)

ceqa-e46b88f975a905a812.name: Driftwood Flats
ceqa-e46b88f975a905a812.description: The project consists of a Major Modification to CP25-0156 to request an additional density bonus incentive/concession/waiver and several design modifications for an affordable residential project with ground floor commercial space that was approved in April 2026. The approved project was found to be exempt under CEQA (Public Resources Code [PRC] section 21080.66). One of the project conditions to meet labor standards specified in section 21080.66(d) now cannot be met, which requires modifications to the approved project conditions of approval. As a result, the former environmental documentation is no longer valid as the project no longer meets all of the requirements set forth in PRC section 21080.66. CEQA review was undertaken for the project in conjunction with the new requests, although the project as approved would not change except for the requested modifications.

ceqa-6e93f0fe37f9522a79.projectTitle: Acquisition of Real Property located at 451 Coast Road, Santa Cruz, California (known as “Coast Road South”)
ceqa-6e93f0fe37f9522a79.description: The project consists of an acquisition of Real Property located at 451 Coast Road in Santa Cruz. The Property consists of two parcels: APNs #059-101-06 and 059-091-15.

ceqa-296bac6b724201c6e2.name: Camp Chesebrough Master Plan Amendment
ceqa-296bac6b724201c6e2.description: The project involves an amendment to the approved master plan at an existing organized camp to allow for the construction of a multiple-use building for training purposes, a shower and restroom building, cabins for short term camping, covered teaching pavilions, a climbing and rappelling tower, a replacement water tank, and a recycling and trash receptacles.

ceqa-92b8ba40313697cbbe.name: Waddell Adaptive Management Plan
ceqa-92b8ba40313697cbbe.agency: California Department of Parks and Recreation
ceqa-92b8ba40313697cbbe.description: Project consists of creating a vegetated foredune at the mouth of Waddell Creek in the Rancho del Oso subunit of Big Basin Redwoods State Park to guide the creek mouth away from public infrastructure, reduce erosion, restore previous lagoon dynamics and alleviate the need for additional hard armoring. Work will occur as follows: •Biologists will survey and clear the work area of any target animal species; •Biological monitors will guide State Park equipment operators tracking onto the beach from the parking lot and begin lowering the sandbar to the south of the current river mouth; •Generated sand will be stockpiled towards the parking lot; •Operators will create a southerly aligned outlet channel with a similar rise and run to the existing northerly channel; •While being shaped, the southern channel will be hydrologically disconnected from the system by a fill plug left in place at the upstream end; •Upon completion of the channel, the upstream sand plug will be removed, allowing water to flow through the southern outlet channel; •Stockpiled sand will then be moved north to construct a foredune between the embayment and the parking lot; •Woody debris will be buried beneath the dune for added support and will remain lower than the parking lot and will mimic previous foredune; and •Seed and plant dune with native plants and water into the dry season as necessary.
ceqa-92b8ba40313697cbbe.crossStreets: Highway 1 and Skyline to the Sea Trail Rd.

ceqa-4bf3f5f9e201254af9.name: Sequoia Group Campground Septic Feasibility Testing
ceqa-4bf3f5f9e201254af9.projectTitle: Sequoia Group Campground Septic Feasibility Testing
ceqa-4bf3f5f9e201254af9.agency: California Department of Parks and Recreation
ceqa-4bf3f5f9e201254af9.description: Project consists of geotechnical testing to evaluate for the installation of new septic restrooms at the Sequoia Group Campground at Big Basin Redwoods State Park to support proposed plans to rebuild the group campground. Within the chosen test location, work will use a rotary auger backhoe attachment and/or manual augers to perform preliminary soil evaluations as follows: •Excavate one (1) 14-ft deep hole for soil profiling; •Excavate four (4) 4-ft to 7-ft deep holes for limited percolation testing; and •Backfill test holes with excavated soils and compact.
ceqa-4bf3f5f9e201254af9.crossStreets: Big Basin Way and North Escape Rd.

ceqa-857b324d3f186c6f43.name: Big Steel Pump Station Fire Hardening
ceqa-857b324d3f186c6f43.projectTitle: Big Steel Pump Station Fire Hardening
ceqa-857b324d3f186c6f43.description: The project will replace the District’s Big Steel booster pump station’s roof and walls with fire-resistant materials. The project involves demolition and removal of the existing wood-framed structure and reconstruction with reinforced concrete masonry unit (CMU) walls, a metal roof, and a perimeter grade beam to support the fire-resistant structure. Fire hardening this booster pump station will mitigate wildfire impacts and improve water supply reliability for the community.

ceqa-02d22c8849aa1fadcf.projectTitle: Wooden Henry Cowell Redwoods State Park Sign at Lockwood Trailhead

ceqa-02d22c8849aa1fadcf.description: Project consists of directly marking the second trailhead to the Sandhills Extension parcel at Henry Cowell Redwoods State Park for the purpose of identifying the area as being within park boundaries. Work will excavate two (2) 2-ft by 3-ft holes, install the new sign, and backfill with concrete to secure.

ceqa-94448473479efea6ee.description: Demolition of an existing single-family dwelling unit and reconstruction of a single-family dwelling unit of similar size and within same footprint and removal of two heritage-sized trees on a parcel located within the Santa Cruz Downtown Historic District.

ceqa-8faac74b0477c068a0.name: 800 West Cliff Drive Roadway Realignment Project
ceqa-8faac74b0477c068a0.projectTitle: 800 West Cliff Drive Roadway Realignment Project
ceqa-8faac74b0477c068a0.description: In December 2023 and early January 2024, high wave and storm events eroded and collapsed a section of the multiuse pathway across from approximately 800 West Cliff Drive and the Light House Field State Beach. The 800 West Cliff Drive Road Realignment project aims to eliminate the weakest link in the West Cliff Drive roadway system as an eroded scarp at the location has encroached to within 21 feet of the existing roadway, partially damaging an adjacent multiuse pathway. The project would shift an approximately 600-foot section of roadway nearest to the scarp approximately 60 feet inland, out of the 100-year erosion zone. A section of the multiuse pathway would also be shifted inland approximately 30 feet. A right-of-way acquisition from State Parks would be required to realign the road and multiuse pathway, as proposed. Other elements of the project include stormwater drainage improvements, minor utility improvements, minor improvements to an existing parking lot, relocation of existing signage and new signage, new fencing, new and relocated benches, removal of existing asphalt along the existing road and multiuse path, and construction site restoration.

ceqa-94fd757436bf30e6c4.name: Envision Peace Village Housing
ceqa-94fd757436bf30e6c4.description: The project consists of a Major Modification to a previously approved application (CP22-0164), revising the previous density bonus request, increasing the total number of residential units from 40 to 47, altering the unit mix, and modifying the building design/envelope. The revised project includes construction of a five-story residential apartment building on a 2.23-acre site. The project would remove 14 heritage trees to construct the apartment complex and associated site improvements.

ceqa-2ffdbf96881d1e400c.name: UC Santa Cruz Wildfire Vegetation Management Project
ceqa-2ffdbf96881d1e400c.description: The California Department of Forestry and Fire Prevention (CAL FIRE) is providing funding to help implement treatments on State Responsibility Area (SRA) lands on the University of California Santa Cruz (UC Santa Cruz), immediately northwest of the city of Santa Cruz, Santa Cruz County. UC Santa Cruz has prepared a Project-Specific Analysis (PSA) and addendum for the project as a later activity covered by the California Vegetation Treatment Project (CalVTP) Program Environmental Impact Report (PEIR) for the UC Santa Cruz Wildfire Vegetation Management Project, which entails implementation of vegetation treatments on up to 2,017 acres; CAL FIRE is providing funding to the Resource Conservation District of Santa Cruz County to implement treatments on up to 165 acres. The proposed treatment types (WUI Fuel Reduction, Fuel Break, and Ecological Restoration) and treatment activities (manual thinning and mastication) are consistent with those evaluated in the CalVTP Program EIR and the writ of mandate issued by the Superior Court of San Diego on November 14, 2025 in California Chaparral Institute and Endangered Habitats League v. Board of Forestry and Fire Protection, and pursuant to PRC § 4483, have been designed to avoid type conversion in areas where chaparral and/or coastal sage scrub plant communities may be present. Maintenance treatments would involve the same vegetation treatment types and activities used in the initial treatments. The purpose of these treatments is to promote forest and watershed health, reduce fuel load, and demonstrate efficacy of climate beneficial prescriptions.

ceqa-3beca53c3b11500eb0.name: San Lorenzo Way Bridge Replacement Project
ceqa-3beca53c3b11500eb0.projectTitle: San Lorenzo Way Bridge Replacement Project
ceqa-3beca53c3b11500eb0.description: The California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) has executed Lake and Streambed Alteration Agreement (EPIMS-SCR-64152-R3), pursuant to Fish and Game Code section 1602, the project Applicant, County of Santa Cruz, Department of Public Works, as represented by Amber Myer. The Project will replace an aging and historic single lane bridge structure (bridge number 36C-0085) carrying San Lorenzo Way over the San Lorenzo River. In addition to replacing the bridge, the proposed Project includes modifications to the bridge approaches to correct the steep grade and improvements at the SR 9/San Lorenzo Way intersection to facilitate merging on and off the highway. The Project also includes using an existing private gravel road as a temporary access road to land uses on the east side of the bridge during construction. All work for the bridge replacement will be outside the ordinary high-water marks of the San Lorenzo River. Project construction activities will be isolated to the upper banks above the San Lorenzo River channel.

ceqa-975ba8815c3dcda802.name: Forest of Nisene Marks State Park Project
ceqa-975ba8815c3dcda802.agency: California Department of Parks and Recreation
ceqa-975ba8815c3dcda802.description: The California Department of Forestry and Fire Prevention (CAL FIRE) is providing funding to help implement treatments on State Responsibility Area (SRA) lands in the Forest of Nisene Marks State Park, north of the city of Aptos, Santa Cruz County. The California Department of Parks and Recreation has prepared a Project-Specific Analysis (PSA) and addendum for the project as a later activity covered by the California Vegetation Treatment Project (CalVTP) Program Environmental Impact Report (PEIR) for the Forest of Nisene Marks State Park Project, which entails implementation of vegetation treatments on up to 9,955 acres; CAL FIRE is providing funding to the Resource Conservation District of Santa Cruz County to implement treatments on up to 220 acres. The proposed treatment types (WUI Fuel Reduction and Ecological Restoration) and treatment activities (manual thinning, mastication, and prescribed burning) are consistent with those evaluated in the CalVTP Program EIR and the writ of mandate issued by the Superior Court of San Diego on November 14, 2025 in California Chaparral Institute and Endangered Habitats League v. Board of Forestry and Fire Protection, and pursuant to PRC § 4483, have been designed to avoid type conversion in areas where chaparral and/or coastal sage scrub plant communities may be present. Maintenance treatments would involve the same vegetation treatment types and activities used in the initial treatments. The purpose of these treatments is to promote forest and watershed health, reduce fuel load, and demonstrate efficacy of climate beneficial prescriptions.

ceqa-2a9ad57d05623dbe16.name: Integrated Ecology, LLC Lease
ceqa-2a9ad57d05623dbe16.agency: California Department of Parks and Recreation
ceqa-2a9ad57d05623dbe16.description: The District seeks to approve a lease agreement with Integrated Ecology, LLC for the use of 0.3 acres at Wilder Ranch State Park for the purpose having a native plant nursery. There will be temporary fencing and shade structures. Integrated Ecology, LLC will use water from State Parks in exchange for plants.

ceqa-f65bdc2b671e87c5c1.name: Study on Rockfish Opsins
ceqa-f65bdc2b671e87c5c1.agency: California Department of Fish and Wildlife, Marine Region 7
ceqa-f65bdc2b671e87c5c1.agencyName: Fish and Wildlife, Region 7 - Marine, Monterey
ceqa-f65bdc2b671e87c5c1.description: The Department of Fish and Wildlife is issuing a permit to Cornell University pursuant to Fish and Game Code Section 2081(a) for educational purposes. The Section 2081(a) permit authorizes the applicant to take coho salmon (Oncorhynchus kisutch), Chinook salmon (O. tshawytscha) and steelhead trout (O. mykiss) during the course of sampling, subject to terms and conditions set forth in the permit. The purpose of this sampling is for the Cornell University’s research study on rockfish opsins. The Section 2081(a) permit authorizes the applicant to potentially capture coho salmon, Chinook salmon, and steelhead trout during surveys. The applicant will conduct yearround research sampling of nearshore rockfish species using hook & line through December 31, 2029.

ceqa-4271af5b811dace987.name: SLVWD Water Storage Tanks Recoating
ceqa-4271af5b811dace987.description: The project consists of the rehabilitation of six above ground water storage tanks ranging from 75,000 to 721,000 gallons capacity in the unincorporated communities of Boulder Creek, Ben Lomond, and Felton. The tanks require recoating to extend their service life. The tank recoating process includes sampling and testing the existing coatings, removal of interior coatings, rewelding damaged metal surfaces, and recoating interior and exterior surfaces. Maintenance, repair, or replacement of tank components or appurtenant structures such as ladders and fences may be needed. Removal of existing tank coatings will follow best management practices and regulatory requirements for any hazardous waste. All work will be limited to existing roads, turnarounds, and within fenced operational areas around tank footprints.

ceqa-1de2c8c6b97bb4e615.name: SLVWD Pasatiempo Wells 7 & 8 Rehabilitation
ceqa-1de2c8c6b97bb4e615.description: The project consists of rehabilitation of two groundwater wells that supply water to over 3,000 residents within portions of the City of Scotts Valley and nearby unincorporated communities. The purpose of the rehabilitation is to restore well efficiency and maintain reliable water production, as Paso 7 is currently under-producing and Paso 8 is inoperable. Rehabilitation activities would include removal of the well pumps, video inspection, mechanical cleaning of the well screens, chemical treatment (acid washing), post-treatment cleaning, disinfection, test pumping, and post-rehabilitation video inspection. Project implementation will require temporary installation of an approximately 2,600-foot-long above-ground pipeline to convey treated water to the nearby Hanson Quarry's drainage pond, where the treated and tested water will be discharged in accordance with regulations.

ceqa-2357fa45abd54533cb.name: 2026 EE36-EE30 Emergency Project
ceqa-2357fa45abd54533cb.description: The project includes repairing an existing failing sewer main after maintenance crews identified structural defects due to age-related deterioration affecting the pipe, joints, and connections that require immediate repair to maintain reliable service

ceqa-d52b1a5042d7c6544f.name: Cliff Drive Resiliency Project
ceqa-d52b1a5042d7c6544f.description: The City of Capitola Public Works Department (City), is proposing a project to address coastal bluff erosion and associated undermining of the roadway along approximately 800 feet of Cliff Drive in Capitola. The proposed restoration project is intended to remediate current bluff erosion and provide resiliency for projected increased erosion associated with climate change/sea-level rise. Bluff erosion has threatened this route since the 1960s and is expected to worsen due to rising sea levels and more intense storms from climate change. The City of Capitola seeks a strategy to manage access along the portion Cliff Drive adjacent to the coastal bluff. In its current configuration Cliff Drive is a busy corridor serving walkers, bicyclists, motorists, and those parking to enjoy the stunning vistas of the Pacific Ocean. Due to the lack of sidewalks along Cliff Drive, conflicts between pedestrians and motorists are possible. The proposed project would include bluff stabilization via a soil-nail-anchored shotcrete wall, rock protection at the base of the bluff, and a resurfaced roadway with two travel lanes, parking and a bike lane. These improvements would be implemented along the nearly 800-foot stretch of Cliff Drive between Portola Drive and Wharf Road in Capitola. This roadway alignment is classified as a minor arterial roadway, and accommodates nearly 8,000 vehicles daily alongside hundreds of bicyclists and pedestrians. It also serves as the primary evacuation route for Capitola Village.
ceqa-d52b1a5042d7c6544f.crossStreets: Cliff Drive between Portola Drive and Wharf Road
ceqa-d52b1a5042d7c6544f.developmentType: Other (Cliff stabilization), Transportation:Other (Roadway stabilization and resurfacing)

ceqa-de2d8313c78f29ea5c.name: 810 3rd Street Site Improvements
ceqa-de2d8313c78f29ea5c.description: The project consists of a Coastal Permit, Administrative Use Permit, and Design Permit to modify an existing parking lot to provide a total of 25 parking spaces, to construct a laundry room addition, conduct utility trenching, and to install a fence on a property with an existing motel use within the boundaries of the Beach South of Laurel Area Plan. ceqa-cd5773a7b8e5e81a89.name: Sunset Processing LLC, CDP 86-0351
ceqa-cd5773a7b8e5e81a89.description: The Department of Cannabis Control, pursuant to authority granted under Business and Procession Code, Section 26012, approved a commercial cannabis processor license submitted on 6/5/2026 by Robert Chen. The project proposes to operate a Class CA indoor co-location cannabis cultivation facility with up to five cultivators on Commercial Agriculture (CA) zoned property, Class 3 manufacturing (volatile extraction) and Class 2 distribution of cannabis product The project includes approximately 590,922 square feet of cultivation within existing greenhouses, manufacturing, processing, distribution, office and storage within an existing 32,458 square foot processing facility on a site containing existing row crops, greenhouse plant production, cannabis cultivation, shipping and office use. Requires a Commercial Development Permit and a Coastal Development Permit Amendment to Permit 86-0351.

ceqa-3cd430220ac822a773.name: SCR 17 PM 7.61 Drainage System Replacement
ceqa-3cd430220ac822a773.agencyName: Caltrans, District 5 - San Luis Obispo/Santa Barbara
ceqa-3cd430220ac822a773.description: Caltrans Geotechnical Design proposes a geotechnical site investigation for the SCR 17 PM 7.61 Drainage System Replacement. The project proposes abandoning an existing culvert with slurry cement and replacing it with a new reinforced concrete pipe culvert. Recommendations for the improvements requires a subsurface investigation to determine the soil and site conditions by drilling vertical soil borings to perform in-situ soil testing utilizing Standard Penetration Tests, collect soil samples for laboratory testing and classification, and developing a subsurface soil profile. The subsurface investigation is also needed to assess the potential for geotechnical hazards associated with the design and construction of the new culvert. All drilling will occur within pavement limits.
ceqa-3cd430220ac822a773.crossStreets: State Route 17 and Vine Hill Road

ceqa-1ad46a7f84c772c7d0.name: Anna Jean Cummings County Park Water Line Replacement Project
ceqa-1ad46a7f84c772c7d0.projectTitle: Anna Jean Cummings County Park Water Line Replacement Project
ceqa-1ad46a7f84c772c7d0.description: Anna Jean Cummings County Park is located at 461 Soquel San Jose Road in Soquel, California (APN 030-341-09). The park is owned and operated by the County of Santa Cruz and provides a variety of recreational amenities including sports fields, playgrounds, picnic areas, restrooms, trails, open space areas, and supporting infrastructure. The park was developed in accordance with the O'Neill Ranch Master Plan and Environmental Impact Report adopted by the County to guide the long-term recreational use and management of the property. Existing utility infrastructure, including domestic water service, supports park operations and visitor-serving facilities throughout the site. The existing domestic waterline serving park facilities has experienced recurring leaks and requires frequent maintenance and repair. The leaks generally occur at intervals corresponding to individual pipe segments located beneath portions of the park entry drive, requiring excavation within paved areas to access and repair the line. To improve long-term reliability, reduce maintenance costs, reduce waste of potable water, and minimize future disruptions to park operations, the County proposes replacing an approximately 1,300-foot-long portion of the existing waterline and relocating portions of the alignment to adjacent landscaped areas where future access and maintenance can be more readily accomplished. The project consists of replacing a portion of the existing domestic water distribution system serving Anna Jean Cummings County Park with approximately 1,300 linear feet of new waterline and associated components installed within previously disturbed and developed portions of the park. The new waterline will connect to the existing system at the southern side of the athletic fields and extend west toward the restroom facility and east toward the restroom and recreational facilities adjacent to the play area. The proposed alignment relocates portions of the existing waterline from beneath the park entry drive into adjacent landscaped and maintained areas to improve accessibility for future maintenance activities, reduce the likelihood of disruptions to park operations, reduce waste of potable water, and improve the long-term reliability of the water system. Project improvements include trench excavation, installation of new waterline, and related utility infrastructure necessary to maintain water service to existing park facilities. The project also includes abandonment of the existing waterline, limited saw-cutting and restoration of sidewalks and paved surfaces where necessary, reconnection to existing facilities, and restoration of all disturbed areas following construction. All work will occur within the boundaries of Anna Jean Cummings County Park and within areas that have been previously developed, landscaped, or otherwise disturbed. The replacement waterline will serve the same park facilities and provide the same purpose and capacity as the existing system. No expansion of park facilities, recreational amenities, or utility service is proposed. No tree removal is anticipated as part of the project, and all disturbed areas will be restored following completion of construction. The project is limited to replacement of the existing domestic waterline and associated utility infrastructure and constitutes the repair, maintenance, minor alteration, and replacement of an existing public utility system involving negligible or no expansion of existing use. Accordingly, the project is exempt pursuant to CEQA Guidelines Sections 15301 (Existing Facilities) and 15302 (Replacement or Reconstruction). The project also includes minor trenching, backfilling, and restoration activities within previously disturbed areas and is therefore exempt pursuant to CEQA Guidelines Section 15304 (Minor Alterations to Land).

ceqa-e8e9ad6dd05da3b252.name: Miller County Park Trails
ceqa-e8e9ad6dd05da3b252.description: Miller County Park is located at 16798 Kings Creek Road near the community of Boulder Creek in unincorporated Santa Cruz County. The park consists of approximately 410 acres across three contiguous parcels (APNs 085-152-05, 085-153-03, and 085-092-08) owned by the County of Santa Cruz and subject to a conservation easement held by Save the Redwoods League. The existing landscape consists of mature redwood forest and riparian habitat adjacent to Kings Creek. The property also includes approximately 2.5 miles of informal trails and an established parking area. The park is currently underutilized, and the existing trail system is in poor condition and in need of maintenance and rehabilitation. The purpose of the project is to improve public access, visitor safety, trail sustainability, and resource protection by formalizing and renovating the existing trail network. The project includes rehabilitation and formalization of the approximately 2.5-mile trail network. Improvements include abandonment and restoration of approximately 1 mile of degraded and unsustainable trail segments. Approximately 1.8 miles of new trail segments will be constructed to replace and bypass the abandoned trail sections while maintaining connectivity within the trail network and improving trail sustainability. The project also includes installation of wayfinding signs, maps, and interpretive displays. Trail improvements may include minor grading (approximately 200 cubic yards), tread improvements, drainage improvements, erosion control measures, revegetation, and related site improvements necessary to support trail construction and restoration activities. The project constitutes minor alterations to existing public facilities involving negligible expansion of use and is therefore exempt pursuant to CEQA Guidelines Section 15301 (Existing Facilities). The project also includes minor alterations to land associated with trail rehabilitation, trail reroutes, restoration activities, drainage improvements, erosion control measures, and revegetation. The project does not involve removal of healthy, mature, or scenic trees and is therefore exempt pursuant to CEQA Guidelines Section 15304 (Minor Alterations to Land). All project activities will be conducted in a manner consistent with the Miller Property Conservation Easement. No healthy, mature redwood trees will be removed as part of the project. The project is limited to trail rehabilitation, trail reroutes, restoration of abandoned trail segments, signage, and associated trail improvements. Future Park improvements not described herein are not included as part of this project. These improvements will enhance trail sustainability, reduce erosion, sedimentation, water quality, and other resource impacts associated with degraded and unsustainable trail segments, and improve public access within an existing county park.

ceqa-66ed4bb9be0104986d.name: Pinto Lake County Park Skatepark
ceqa-66ed4bb9be0104986d.description: The project consists of the construction of a new skatepark and associated site improvements at Pinto Lake County Park, including modification of an existing biofiltration planter along Green Valley Road to comply with County Design Criteria (CDC) stormwater requirements. The skatepark will provide a public recreational facility serving County residents and park visitors. Associated improvements include removal of an existing asphalt path, installation of a cobble-lined swale and area drains to convey runoff to the modified biofiltration planter, and implementation of Low Impact Development (LID) measures and Best Management Practices (BMPs) to minimize hydrologic and pollutant impacts. The total new and replaced impervious area associated with the project is 9,733 square feet, classifying the project as a Large Project under the County Design Criteria and triggering full LID and BMP compliance requirements. The biofiltration planter will be redesigned to provide stormwater treatment and detention consistent with CDC requirements, including detention of runoff from the 10-year, 15-minute storm event at the 5-year pre-development release rate, as required for projects within the Salsipuedes Creek Watershed. To accommodate the proposed skatepark, three (3) mature London Plane trees will be removed as part of site preparation. All remaining on-site trees will be protected in place pursuant to the recommendations of a certified arborist retained for the project. In response to the tree removals, six (6) new trees will be planted on-site, representing a net gain in tree canopy. In addition, all biofiltration planters and associated landscape areas will be planted with 100% native understory species, enhancing habitat value, supporting local pollinators, and reducing long-term landscape maintenance needs. The skatepark footprint will be constructed on areas currently occupied by unused turf grass that required irrigation to maintain. The replacement of non-functional turf with the skatepark hardscape and native plantings will result in overall water savings, consistent with the County's water conservation goals and the State's urban water use reduction objectives. The remainder of the site will be retained in its natural state, further minimizing the project's environmental footprint.

ceqa-891c375f5e29ee142f.name: Castro Adobe State Historic Park Accessibility Improvements
ceqa-891c375f5e29ee142f.projectTitle: Castro Adobe State Historic Park Accessibility Improvements
ceqa-891c375f5e29ee142f.agency: California Department of Parks and Recreation
ceqa-891c375f5e29ee142f.description: Project consists of removing barriers and providing improved access to existing day use facilities at Rancho San Andreas Castro Adobe Park Property to better accommodate visitors with disabilities. Work will: • Construct an accessible concrete parking stall and access ramp to the front entry of the Kimbro House; • Construct an accessible path of travel from the Kimbro House Courtyard to the front of the Castro Adobe with two (2) landings for installation of interpretive signage; • On the front and side exteriors, minimally excavate to construct a timber-edged aggregate paved area for a firm and stable surface for large tour groups to congregate; • Provide an access ramp to the existing wooden deck in front of Adobe; and • Using materials matching the existing deck/boardwalk, construct a new low-profile deck in front of the Cocina entrance to establish a flush entry into the exhibit area.

ceqa-8a9c723eb16f8e6b49.name: Flock Safety Automated License Plate Reading (ALPR) Camera Installation
ceqa-8a9c723eb16f8e6b49.description: The project consists of the installation of Flock Safety automated license plate reading (ALPR) cameras on behalf of the Watsonville Police Department at multiple locations within public right-of-way. The project includes mounting ALPR camera and solar equipment to existing traffic signal or streetlight poles at certain locations, and installation of new breakaway support poles with small concrete foundations at other locations where existing infrastructure is not available. The purpose of the installation is to assist law enforcement in identifying vehicles associated with criminal activity. The beneficiaries of the project include law enforcement and the public at large, as the installation supports public safety objectives within the City of Watsonville.

ceqa-7840415f9810111930.name: 2026 Annual Code Update
ceqa-7840415f9810111930.description: On June 30, 2026, the County of Santa Cruz approved a project amending various chapters of the Santa Cruz County Code, making minor General Plan Map Amendments, and amending the Zoning Map to streamline provisions to ensure compliance with applicable State and Federal law, and improve clarity, accuracy, and internal consistency. ceqa-721f73d51c31992f98.projectTitle: Big Basin Redwoods State Park General Plan Supplemental EIR for the Reimagining Big Basin Redwoods State Park Facilities Management Plan and General Plan

ceqa-4b29c125343cc2a8b1.name: 800 West Cliff Drive Roadway Realignment Project
ceqa-4b29c125343cc2a8b1.projectTitle: 800 West Cliff Drive Roadway Realignment Project
ceqa-4b29c125343cc2a8b1.description: In December 2023 and early January 2024, high wave and storm events eroded and collapsed a section of the multiuse pathway across from approximately 800 West Cliff Drive and the Light House Field State Beach. The 800 West Cliff Drive Road Realignment project aims to eliminate the weakest link in the West Cliff Drive roadway system as an eroded scarp at the location has encroached to within 21 feet of the existing roadway, partially damaging an adjacent multiuse pathway. The project would shift an approximately 600-foot section of roadway nearest to the scarp approximately 60 feet inland, out of the 100-year erosion zone. A section of the multiuse pathway would also be shifted inland approximately 30 feet. A right-of-way acquisition from State Parks would be required to realign the road and multiuse pathway, as proposed.

ceqa-57125d66e38d159b35.name: 307 Chestnut Street Residence
ceqa-57125d66e38d159b35.description: Demolition of an existing single-family dwelling unit and reconstruction of a single-family dwelling unit of similar size and within same footprint and removal of two heritage-sized trees on a parcel located within the Santa Cruz Downtown Historic District.

ceqa-440b6242cf61f20782.name: Crestwood Heights Water Association Water System Consolidation Project
ceqa-440b6242cf61f20782.projectTitle: Crestwood Heights Water Association Water System Consolidation Project
ceqa-440b6242cf61f20782.description: The proposed project involves consolidation of the Crestwood Heights Water Association water system with the City of Watsonville municipal water system. Improvements include installation of new water mains, service laterals, and meters for approximately 45 residences, system interties, and removal of existing water system infrastructure. In total, the proposed project would include 7,000 linear feet (1.33 miles) of new pipelines. The proposed project would install water mains within the right-of-way of Lakeview Road, Cambridge Drive, Kingston Drive, Oxford Drive, Strafford Drive, and Crestwood Drive. The proposed project also involves preparing a Drinking Water State Revolving Fund application to assist in funding construction of the proposed project.
ceqa-440b6242cf61f20782.crossStreets: State Route 129 (Riverside Road) and Lakeview Road

ceqa-b486686c037cb6d243.name: 375 Technology Drive - Hotel Project
ceqa-b486686c037cb6d243.description: The project includes construction of a 72,348-square foot, five-story, 70-foot-tall Holiday Inn Express hotel containing 95 rooms. The project includes 100 parking spaces, 80 of which will utilize mechanical stacking devices. The project also includes a request to amend Watsonville Municipal Code Section 14-16.505(c) - "Other Requirements" to include a 75-foot maximum height limit for hotel uses and a request for a variance for the front yard setbacks.

ceqa-fd624156e1bd88fa02.name: Floral Drive Water Main Replacement
ceqa-fd624156e1bd88fa02.description: The Floral Drive Water Main Replacement Project will replace 1,350 linear feet of existing water main with a new 6” PVC water main between 34th Avenue and 38th Avenue in the Pleasure Point area of unincorporated Santa Cruz County. There will be one new hydrant installed at 35th Ave and Floral Dr. The installation trench will be restored with asphalt, type 2 slurry seal, and thermoplastic striping per County of Santa Cruz standards.
ceqa-fd624156e1bd88fa02.crossStreets: Floral Drive between 34th Avenue and 38th Avenue

ceqa-f144cbcb4b31b5cc5e.name: Ordinances Related to Protections Against On-Shore Support Facilities for Off-Shore Oil and Gas or Deep-Sea Mining or Exploration
ceqa-f144cbcb4b31b5cc5e.projectTitle: Ordinances Related to Protections Against On-Shore Support Facilities for Off-Shore Oil and Gas or Deep-Sea Mining or Exploration
ceqa-f144cbcb4b31b5cc5e.description: The project consists of two ordinances (2026-12 and 2026-13) amending the Santa Cruz Municipal Code (SCMC) and the City's Local Coastal Program. Ordinance 2026-13 would add Section 24.06.093 to Chapter 24.06 - Zoning Map and Text Amendments and amend Sections 24.06.090 and 24.10.1620. These changes would add protections against on-shore facilities supporting off-shore oil and gas drilling and deep-sea mining and exploration. Ordinance 2026-12 would amend SCMC Section 24.10.1525, which is part of the City's Local Coastal Program Implementation Plan, to extend existing land-use prohibitions to on-shore facilities supporting deep-sea mining and exploration. In addition, the ordinances add science-backed findings related to the ecological, public health, economic, and climate impacts related to oil and gas drilling and deep-sea mining and exploration. The two ordinances make the following changes to the SCMC: • Add definitions of related terms for clarity and specificity within the municipal code; • Update the existing requirement that any zoning change to accommodate on-shore support facilities for off-shore oil and gas drilling be subject to a vote of the people to also require that any zoning change to accommodate on-shore support facilities for deep-sea mining and exploration be subject to a vote of the people; and • Add prohibitions against on-shore support facilities for deep-sea mining, in addition to the existing prohibitions against on-shore support facilities for off-shore oil and gas drilling, to the City's General Industrial and General Industrial/Performance Districts.

ceqa-d919397ed0564ad1fc.name: Peavine Water Pipeline Replacement Project
ceqa-d919397ed0564ad1fc.description: The SLVWD watershed and water system were severely impacted and damaged by the CZU Lightning Complex Wildfire in 2020, including the Peavine pipeline. The Peavine Water Pipeline Replacement Project (project) involves replacement of the approximately 1.2-mile-long Peavine pipeline with new HDPE pipe.

ceqa-21465a224f550826d0.name: 2050 Metropolitan Transportation Plan/Sustainable Communities Strategy and 2050 Regional Transportation Plans for San Benito, Santa Cruz, and Monterey Counties
ceqa-21465a224f550826d0.projectTitle: 2050 Metropolitan Transportation Plan/Sustainable Communities Strategy and 2050 Regional Transportation Plans for San Benito, Santa Cruz, and Monterey Counties

The 2050 RTP will guide the development of transportation projects and programs throughout Santa Cruz County. The 2050 MTP/SCS EIR serves as the EIR for the 2050 MTP/SCS and for the 2050 RTP for Santa Cruz County.

ceqa-43cbc9eeef687543e7.name: SR-1 Wildlife Crossing
ceqa-43cbc9eeef687543e7.agencyName: Caltrans, District 5 - San Luis Obispo/Santa Barbara
ceqa-43cbc9eeef687543e7.description: Caltrans Geotechnical Design proposes a geotechnical site investigation for the SR-1 Wildlife Crossing, located on State Route 1 (SR-1) at PM 5.11 in Santa Cruz County. Trenchless culvert installation requires a subsurface investigation to evaluate subsurface site conditions by drilling vertical borings, performing in-situ soil testing, and confirming soil and rock conditions for use in design. A total of six borings will be advanced: five through pavement into soil and rock, and one through a dirt road in the median into soil and rock. The proposed borings would be four to six inches in diameter and extend between 30 and 40 feet below the ground surface, depending on the location. Once the borings are completed, each hole will be backfilled following appropriate procedures. Typically, the backfill material is a neat cement and/or bentonite (clay).It may take up to three weeks to complete the investigation. Work is anticipated to occur at night. Drilling activities will occur during dry weather only, June through October. Precautions during drilling will be employed to minimize the potential for equipment leaks or drilling fluid spillage. All borings will be drilled within State Right-of-Way (ROW), accessible from the northbound and southbound travel lanes of SR-1, the median, or in the paved or unvegetated shoulder.

ceqa-e2e74d817d354d9f7c.name: Lower Wilder Ranch Trail Restoration
ceqa-e2e74d817d354d9f7c.agency: California Department of Parks and Recreation
ceqa-e2e74d817d354d9f7c.description: Project proposes to improve existing trail alignments within Wilder Ranch State Park to reduce user conflict and improve trail safety. The work is proposed for portions of the Eucalyptus Loop, Old Cabin, and Wild Boar Trails will alleviate erosion, reduce sediment delivery into nearby drainages, and curtail the creation of unofficial trail segments used to bypass trail obstacles. Work will occur as follows: On the Fern Grotto Beach Access • Remove one (1) wood puncheon; • Remove approx. 50 linear feet (LF) of poorly aligned and redundant trail; and • Construct 30 LF of wood cabling steps leading down existing trail to beach. On the Eucalyptus Loop Trail: • Construct an approx. 6,000 LF reroute of the eastern segment of the road and construct a new approx. 4ft wide trail on contour under forest canopy; • Remove approx. 5,000 LF of poorly aligned road in the meadow and topographically Restore approx. 59,510 sq ft of the meadow; • Excavate approx. 300 cu. ft. to install concrete abutments and approaches for five (5) steel I-beam bridges and one (1) wood puncheon. • Construct approx. 170 ft of 6ft wide drainage lens along trail (5 locations); and • Reconstruct sections of the trail with corrected outslope to facilitate proper drainage. On the Old Cabin Trail: • Construct an approx. 3,750 LF reroute to pull the existing trail off the ridge line and away from the water course; • Remove approx. 3,500 LF of poorly aligned trail and topographically restore the area • Excavate approx. 68 cu. ft. for concrete abutments and approaches for one (1) steel I-beam bridge and one (1) wood puncheon; and • Reconstruct sections of the trail with corrected outslope to facilitate proper drainage. On the Wild Boar Trail: • Construct an approx. 2,400 LF reroute to pull existing trail out of the meadow and off of the fall line; • Remove approx. 2,210 LF of poorly aligned road and restore the meadow and forest understory; • Construct a 75ft long x 6ft wide drainage lens along the trail; and • Reconstruct sections of the trail with corrected outslope to facilitate proper drainage.

ceqa-55e6994a3affccc605.name: Approval of Local Energy Efficiency and Conservation Standards Application Findings Submitted by the City of Santa Cruz for the 2025 Energy Code Cycle.
ceqa-55e6994a3affccc605.projectTitle: Approval of Local Energy Efficiency and Conservation Standards Application Findings Submitted by the City of Santa Cruz for the 2025 Energy Code Cycle.
ceqa-55e6994a3affccc605.description: The California Energy Commission (CEC) adopts and regularly updates regulations that define a process for local governments to apply to the CEC to make certain findings regarding locally adopted energy conservation or energy insulation standards (California Code of Regulations (CCR), Title 24, Part 1, section 10-106 and section 10-110; Public Resources Code (PRC) section 25402.1(h)(2)). The local government’s proposed standards are often referred to as the Local Reach Codes and require local governments to submit an application to the CEC consistent with the requirements listed in section 10-106(b). Before the local standards may be enforced, the CEC must make the following findings pursuant to PRC section 25402.1(h)(2) and as listed in section 10-106(a): 1) The proposed local standards will require the diminution of energy consumption levels compared to the 2025 Energy Code, and 2) The local government has filed the basis of its cost-effectiveness determination with the CEC. On December 30, 2026, the City of Santa Cruz (the City) submitted an application to the CEC that included: 1) the basis of its determination that the locally adopted energy efficiency standards contained in Ordinance No. 2025-22 are cost-effective; and (2) documentation that the locally adopted energy efficiency standards contained in Ordinance No.2025-22 will require the diminution of energy consumption levels compared to the 2025 Building Energy Efficiency Standards (Energy Code), as required by PRC section 25402.1(h)(2) and by CCR, Title 24, Part 1, section 10-106. Based on the information submitted, staff analysis, and the Executive Director's recommendation, the CEC approved findings of the City’s section 10-106 application at the CEC’s May 26, 2026, Business Meeting.

ceqa-79d837b3f31dd3c60d.projectTitle: Atkinson Lane Integrated Flood Management and Watershed Restoration Project - Phase I - Native Habitat Restoration
ceqa-79d837b3f31dd3c60d.description: The proposed project includes implementation of approximately 4.0 acres of native habitat restoration around the wetland complex located at 78 Atkinson Lane. Work will involve removal of non-native invasive species, including removal and treatment of approximately 2.0 acres of Himalayan blackberry infestation, planting native plants, and installation of erosion control. Restoration treatment areas for Phase I are outlined in Attachment A. Work will be carried out principally with hand labor. Existing native trees and shrubs will be preserved and protected in place. Protective measures including worker training, surveys prior to work commencement, and daily monitoring will be implemented to ensure that the habitat restoration activities will not result in adverse impacts on any native wildlife species or their habitats.
