ceqa-b1c571d25158a47906.description: The project involves a minor operational change at the City of Santa Cruz Resource Recovery Facility (RRF), located at 605 Dimeo Lane. The RRF is located approximately three miles west of the city limits off Highway 1 and encompasses approximately 100 acres; see Figure 1. The facility serves as the City's primary solid waste management and recycling facility, and currently accepts, processes, and transfers municipal solid waste, recyclables, and organic materials. The RRF currently operates seven days a week, opening at 6:00 AM for City trucks and landfill and ancillary operations, with public access beginning at 7:30 AM, pursuant to terms of its operating permit from the California Department of Resources Recycling and Recovery (CalRecycle) (Solid Waste Facility Permit No. 44-AA-0001). Current permitted hours require ancillary operations, including removing daily cover, to begin at the same time City trucks arrive, causing delays while trucks wait for the site to be prepared. The project would shift the ancillary operations start time from 6:00 AM to 5:00 AM, allowing sufficient time of site preparation before trucks arrive and improving overall coordination and traffic flow at the facility.

ceqa-ca25ecfe1ebe8a6eef.name: Santa Cruz Resource Recovery Facility Enclosed Flare Station Installation Project
ceqa-ca25ecfe1ebe8a6eef.projectTitle: Santa Cruz Resource Recovery Facility Enclosed Flare Station Installation Project
ceqa-ca25ecfe1ebe8a6eef.description: Project Description: The project consists of installation of an enclosed low-nitrogen oxide (Nox) flare to act as the backup landfill gas collection and destruction device for the existing onsite landfill gas collection system and Landfill Gas to Energy (LFGTE) Plant. The purpose of this improvement is to establish a permanent backup flare facility to collect methane gas and burn under regulatory provisions of the Monterey Bay Air Resources District (MBARD) in the event that the LFGTE is temporarily shut down. The facility would be located immediately west of the existing LFGTE Plant. The project includes construction of an approximately 3,600-square-foot flare station, which would house the low NOx flare station equipment, including the enclosed flare stack, an air compressor, three blowers, a condensate management system, and the equipment control panel. The station would be situated on a concrete pad and would be accessed by an existing landfill road. A three-foot tall concrete retaining wait would be installed on the northern boundary of the new station. The project also includes: • Installation of approximately 200 linear feet of landfill gas header pipe to connect the new flare station to the existing LFGTE Plant. • Installation of a line to tie into the air and condensate management lines from the fla re station to the existing LFGTE infrastructure on site. • Trenching and installing new electrical feed to the flare station, wiring, conduits, and associated electrical components. • Installation of the 6-foot-high chain link fence and access gates around the new station. Background. The City of Santa Cruz (City) Resource Recovery Facility (RRF) is required to have a landfill gas (LFG) collection and control system that continuously extracts gas from the landfill and sends it to a control device such as a flare or engine. To meet this requirement, the City has contracted with a third-party vendor for over 20 years to operate the LFGTE Plant to collect and convert landfill gas into electricity which is sent back into the PG&E grid. In early 2024, the LFGTE Plant was shut down, at no fault of the City or its vendor, due to damage to PG&E's electrical infrastructure from a February 2024 storm event, which has since been declared as state and federal natural disasters. Given the uncertainty of PG&E's timeline for repair, the City installed a temporary flare for the landfill to re-start collecting and burning LFG given the potential environmental and health and safety risks associated with uncollected LFG. To ensure safety, the City has been monitoring landfill gas migration since the shutdown, and in May 2024 obtained approval from MBARD to operate the temporary flare as a backup LFG destruction device until a permanent flare could be installed. The temporary flare, which is located next to the LFGTE Plant, was installed and began operating in May 2024 until the LFGTE resumed operation in July 2024. The existing, temporary open flare was meant to be a backup to continue collecting and destroying LFG when the LFGTE Plant is down. It is currently operating under a variance issued by MBARD as the LFGTE plant's backup device and must be removed by July 2026. The new flare would provide a permanent backup to maintain continuous collection and destruction of LFG and prevent the City from violating state law and conditions of the RRF permits. A location for installation of the permanent enclosed flare station was identified near the existing LFGTE Plant. The project location was chosen due to proximity to the LFGTE Plant to reduce the amount of piping required to connect the two systems; proximity to electrical utilities to reduce the amount of trenching and power utility installation; and ability of the flare stack to maintain required clearances.

The scope of site work includes improvements to the accessible path of travel throughout the campus and a new accessible ramp leading to the existing playground. The Project will include approximately 23,700 square feet of existing classroom building modernization, including fire alarm upgrades for the full campus. Athletic facilities will include renovation of the softball field and running track. Parking areas will be reconfigured, and new electrical service and fire alarm upgrades will be extended throughout the site. Existing landscape retaining walls (less than 4' in height) will be repaired in specific areas around the playground. Scope of work will include new fencing, a backup generator and enclosure, provision for a future battery energy storage system, and existing restroom upgrades. Site alterations include campus wide upgrades to fire alarm, electrical, and audio- visual system infrastructure. Classroom building upgrades include lighting, casework, signage, hardware, and interior finishes. In addition to the Sitework and Building Modernization projects, a domestic water infrastructure project is to be included. These improvements consist of new water storage tanks, new pressure pumps, a distribution system, fire hydrants, controls, and appurtenances. A retaining wall and concrete pad will support the new tanks. Gravel paving, fencing, gates, and storm drainage improvements, and demolition of existing systems are included.

ceqa-0bd59573b02e42c535.name: 5-Mile Pipeline Shaded Fuel Break
ceqa-0bd59573b02e42c535.description: The project will create an approximately 2.2-mile shaded fuel break along SLVWD’s 5-Mile Pipeline and approximately 1 mile of shaded fuel break along Pipeline access roads. The Pipeline provides a critical fuel break location, directly protecting the community of Boulder Creek and the District's Lyon Water Treatment Plant. The project will reduce fire hazards along the Pipeline and access roads, reduce the vertical and horizontal continuity of vegetative fuel, improve ingress for emergency response services, improve retained tree health, and enhance resilience to future wildfire. Mechanical and manual treatment will increase the horizontal and vertical canopy separation. Nesting bird surveys will be performed if work is to be performed during nesting bird season. Biomass will be piled, chipped, and/or lopped and scattered to specifications. Following the initial treatment, maintenance of the shaded fuel break will be performed on a regular basis.

ceqa-e12b2e7ef93c6205c2.name: 375 Technology Drive - Hotel Project
ceqa-e12b2e7ef93c6205c2.description: The project site is a vacant, approximately 1.1-acre parcel located at 375 Technology Drive (APN: 015-101-67) near Westgate Drive and Highway 1 in the western portion of the City. The project includes construction of a 72,348-square foot, five-story, 70-foot-tall Holiday Inn Express hotel containing 95 rooms. The project includes surface parking for 50 spaces at the rear (south side) of the site and 50 parking spaces located underneath the building, both of which will utilize mechanical stacking devices. ceqa-1016a67e6b00966334.name: Capitola Road at Leona Creek Culvert Rehabilitation Project
ceqa-1016a67e6b00966334.projectTitle: Capitola Road at Leona Creek Culvert Rehabilitation Project
ceqa-1016a67e6b00966334.description: The proposed project will rehabilitate the lower 100 lineal feet of a 66-inch corrugated metal culvert pipe. The culvert is located below Capitola Road and on private property within drainage easements. The total length of the culvert is 216 feet. The culvert conveys Leona Creek which drains into Schwan Lagoon. The project will take place between July 1st and September 30th with an expected construction duration of five days, and a maximum dewatered period of fourteen days. Temporary diversion dams composed of clean gravel and visqueen sheeting will be installed at the upstream and downstream ends of the culvert. Creek flow at the upstream dam will be pumped through rigid or flexible pipe to an adjacent sanitary sewer manhole. Nuisance water from the work area that collects upstream of the downstream dam will be pumped through rigid or flexible pipe to a tank and then disposed into the sanitary sewer system. Once the work area is isolated from the creek, the culvert interior will be cleaned, and any voids will be filled with a repair mortar. Exterior voids around the culvert will be compaction grouted from the pipe interior with polyurethane geotechnical foam. A 1.5-inch layer and 1.0-inch layer of fiber reinforced grout will be applied to the pipe interior and lower corroded portion of manholes within the culvert using a centrifugally cast concrete pipe machine. Once the concrete has cured (typically 72 hours) the creek diversion will be removed.

ceqa-ee798a7f41cb0a4d6d.name: UC Santa Cruz Wildfire Vegetation Management Project
ceqa-ee798a7f41cb0a4d6d.description: UC Santa Cruz proposes to implement vegetation treatments on up to 2,017 acres, of which 274 acres are in the California Coastal Zone, on the Main Residential Campus in Santa Cruz County. UC Santa Cruz has prepared a Project-Specific Analysis and Addendum (PSA/Addendum) for the project as a later activity covered by the California Vegetation Treatment Project (CalVTP) Program Environmental Impact Report (EIR). UC Santa Cruz Main Residential Campus and the surrounding area have experienced a legacy of intensive land uses paired with a subsequent period of lack of disturbance. This has resulted in very high forest densities, significant accumulations of live and dead fuels, significant changes to wildlife habitats, shifts in historic pathways of ecological succession, lowered biodiversity, and heightened fire risk to developed communities. The proposed treatment types are ecological restoration, wildland-urban interface (WUI) fuel reduction, and maintenance of existing fuel breaks (shaded and non-shaded). The proposed treatment activities consist of manual vegetation treatments, mechanical vegetation treatments, prescribed burning (broadcast burning, pile burning, and cultural burning), targeted herbicide application, and prescribed herbivory (predominantly with goats or sheep). The objectives of the proposed project broadly are to steward natural resources in a manner that aligns with campus values of biodiversity, resiliency, sustainability, traditional ecological knowledge, unique campus integrity, and the overall academic mission. The specific goals of the proposed project are to establish ecosystem and campus community resilience while promoting biodiversity as well as restore degraded habitats and protect sensitive resources including valuable coastal ecosystems.

ceqa-18f60e9df0da2c4cee.description: The proposed project will establish a shaded fuel break along the Mount Hermon Association property adjacent to Graham Hill Road. Approximately 29 acres of roadside understory will be thinned within 500 feet of the Mount Hermon property along Graham Hill Road. Project crews will selectively remove small-diameter trees, shrubs, and ladder fuels to reduce vertical and horizontal fuel continuity and roadside fire hazards. Treatments will focus primarily on conifers and hardwoods less than 12 inches DBH, while also addressing dead or hazardous trees that pose safety risks. Downed material larger than 12 inches in diameter will be retained on site to maintain habitat and soil health.

ceqa-f55bce188864c9bfe2.description: The proposed project would readopt the emergency regulations which rescinded the commercial 20-fathom depth constraint and extended federal trip limits for non-nearshore groundfish into state waters north of 37° 07' N latitude. The proposed project would also keep in place the prohibition on the commercial take of quillback rockfish, statewide. The proposed project would readopt the emergency regulations which rescinded the commercial 20-fathom depth constraint and extended federal trip limits for non-nearshore groundfish into state waters north of 37° 07' N latitude. The proposed project would also keep in place the prohibition on the commercial take of quillback rockfish, statewide. The purpose of the proposed project is to restore access to fishing grounds based upon updated scientific stock assessment information for the quillback rockfish stock off California. The current unwarranted restrictions constrain commercial fishing efforts to a limited area of the State’s waters. The proposed regulations would remove these unneeded constraints, and be consistent with anticipated federal regulatory actions, thereby distributing effort and pressure on groundfish stocks, in both federal and State waters. Additionally, adoption of scientifically-based seasons, depth constraints, and commercial trip limits provides for the maintenance of sufficient populations of quillback rockfish and other groundfish to ensure their continued existence. Overall, the proposed actions preserves natural resources and is protective of the environment.

ceqa-17c7c4ba778def87f2.name: Approval of Local Energy Efficiency and Conservation Standards Application Findings Submitted by the City of Santa Cruz for the 2025 Energy Code Cycle
ceqa-17c7c4ba778def87f2.projectTitle: Approval of Local Energy Efficiency and Conservation Standards Application Findings Submitted by the City of Santa Cruz for the 2025 Energy Code Cycle
ceqa-17c7c4ba778def87f2.description: The California Energy Commission (CEC) adopts and regularly updates regulations that define a process for local governments to apply to the CEC to make certain findings regarding locally adopted energy conservation or energy insulation standards (CCR, Title 24, Part 1, section 10-106 and section 10-110; Public Resources Code section 25402.1(h)(2)). The local government’s proposed standards are often referred to as the Local Reach Codes and require local governments submit an application to the CEC consistent with the requirements listed in section 10-106(b). Before the local standards may be enforced, the CEC must make two non-discretionary findings pursuant to PRC section 25402.1(h)(2) and as listed in section 10-106(a): 1) The proposed local standards will require the diminution of energy consumption levels compared to the 2022 Energy Code, and 2) The local government has filed the basis of its cost-effectiveness determination with the CEC. On 22nd September, 2025, the City of Santa Cruz (the City) submitted an application to the CEC that included: 1) the basis of its determination that the locally adopted energy efficiency standards contained in Ordinance No. 2025-19 are cost-effective; and (2) documentation that the locally adopted energy efficiency standards contained in Ordinance No. 2025-19 will require the diminution of energy consumption levels compared to the 2025 Building Energy Efficiency Standards (Energy Code), as required by PRC section 25402.1(h)(2) and by CCR, Title 24, Part 1, section 10-106 (section 10-106). Based on the information submitted, staff analysis, and the Executive Director's recommendation, the CEC approved findings of the City’s section 10-106 application at the CEC’s January 21, 2026, Business Meeting.

ceqa-eb081292e37dbfe5de.projectTitle: Beltz 10 Aquifer Storage and Recovery & Beltz 11 Well Injection Pilot Tests
ceqa-eb081292e37dbfe5de.description: The City of Santa Cruz Water Department is seeking to pilot test aquifer storage and recovery and well injection at its existing Beltz 10 well facility, which has two wells on site, Beltz 10 and Beltz 11, as part of a feasibility study to assess the viability of diverting excess surface water to the Santa Cruz Mid County Groundwater Basin. The Beltz 10 pilot test requires installing a monitoring well at the City's existing Beltz 10 well facility. The pilot testing is expected to last up to 150 days from 2026 to 2027. The City of Santa Cruz Water Department is seeking to pilot test aquifer storage and recovery (ASR) and well injection at its existing Beltz 10 well facility, which has two wells on site, Beltz 10 and Beltz 11 , as part of a feasibility study to assess the viability of diverting excess surface water to the Santa Cruz Mid County Groundwater Basin. The Beltz 10 well facility is shown on figure one. The ASR pilot testing of the Beltz 10 well seeks to field demonstrate the potential application of ASR in the in the A/AA unit Purisima Aquifer system. A new monitoring well will be installed as part of this work. The injection pilot testing of the Beltz 11 well seeks to investigate the potential to raise water levels in the Tu aquifer. The pilot testing results will be used to assess viability of the storage of drinking water underground at the Beltz 10 well facility and will provide the basis for the design and permitting for a long-term full-scale ASR and/or well.injection project. Preparation of Beltz 10 and Beltz 11 wells for pilot testing will include downhole cleaning procedures and modifications to the wells to establish a connection to the distribution system, retain or exchange pumps and add appurtenances. The ASR pilot test at Beltz 10 requires installing a monitoring well at the City's existing Beltz 10 well facility. This new monitoring well will be used to collect water level and water quality data. The monitoring well will be 2.5 inches in diameter. Drilling will be performed using the direct rotary method with bentonite-based fluid, which will be hauled offsite for disposal. Higher turbidity discharges from well development will be routed to the to the Beltz Water Treatment Plant (Beltz WTP) reclaim tank, which drains to the sanitary sewer system. Lower turbidity discharges from well development will be routed via the existing raw water pipeline to the unnamed creek at 30th Ave, a tributary to Moran Lake. A monitoring well vault and manhole will be installed to provide access for instrumentation, monitoring, or sampling. All construction activities will occur during working hours Monday through Friday 8am to 5pm consistent with County noise ordinance requirements. Construction of the monitoring well will require 12 working days. Some tree limbs will be required to be removed to allow the drill rig to access the site. The ASR pilot test at Beltz 10 will involve three repeated injection storage and recovery cycles with increasing quantities of water. Cycle 1 is expected to recover about 0.44 million gallons (mg). Cycle 2 is expected to recover about 3 mg. Water from Cycles 1 and 2 will be routed via the existing raw water pipeline to the unnamed creek at 30th Ave, a tributary to Moran Lake. Cycle 3 injection operations, if water quality pilot testing results from Cycles 1 and 2 are favorable, will result in the recovery of 13 mg that will be treated at the Beltz WTP will go into the distribution system. Water levels will be monitored after recovery. The injection pilot test at Beltz 11 will involve two repeated injection storage and recovery cycles at with increasing quantities of water extracted after injection. Cycle 1 is expected to recover about 0.1 million gallons (mg). Cycle 2 is expected to recover about 1 mg. Cycle 3 injection operations, if water quality pilot testing results from Cycles 1 and 2 are favorable, will result in the storage of 10 mg. Water levels at an existing monitoring well will be monitored to assess the response to injection at Beltz 11. Noise typical of existing operation noise will occur during pilot testing. The pilot testing is expected to last up to 150 days from 2026 to 2027.

ceqa-08dba5d826469b83a8.name: 2025 Scotts Valley Town Center Specific Plan Update
ceqa-08dba5d826469b83a8.projectTitle: 2025 Scotts Valley Town Center Specific Plan
ceqa-08dba5d826469b83a8.description: The purpose of the Plan is to create a vision, policies, and objective standards to guide new development within the Plan area in a way that supports existing and new businesses, residents, and the overall community. The Plan would manage and direct changes in development patterns within the Plan area through 2045 and guide present and future land uses, development intensity and scale, urban design, economic development, circulation management and mobility, infrastructure and public services, and community benefits. The project will allow for up to 657 residential units (consistent with the City’s Housing Element), up to 82,000 square feet of commercial uses, and up to 35,000 square feet of public/civic uses. The project will include adoption of amendments to the City’s General Plan and Zoning Ordinance, changing certain existing land use designations in the Plan Area, creating new zoning districts, and updating existing or establishing new development standards to replace some of the current zoning provisions applicable to the Plan Area.

ceqa-3f85830efde961506f.name: Inland Big Basin Redwoods State Park Forest Health and Resilience Project
ceqa-3f85830efde961506f.agency: California Department of Parks and Recreation
ceqa-3f85830efde961506f.description: Coastal Conservancy grant to Sempervirens Fund to conduct the Big Basin Redwood Wildfire Resilience Project consists of vegetation treatments and habitat enhancement on 215 acres in the old-growth coast redwood area of Big Basin Redwood State Park in Santa Cruz County. The Big Basin Redwood Wildfire Resilience Project is addressed in the Inland Big Basin Redwoods State Park Forest Health Project Specific Analysis and Addendum. California Department of Parks and Recreation's Inland Big Basin Redwoods State Park Forest Health Project Specific Analysis and Addendum proposes to implement vegetation treatments and maintenance on up to 9,977.25 acres of land within the eastern and inland portion of Big Basin Redwoods State Park in Santa Cruz and San Mateo Counties. California State Parks prepared a Project Specific Analysis and CEQA Addendum to evaluate if the project is within the scope of the CalVTP PEIR, and consider revisions or changes to the PEIR that would expand its coverage to include all project areas and provide information on the proposed project. Treatment types include ecological restoration. Treatment activities include prescribed burning, manual, mechanical, and targeted herbicide applications. The Inland Big Basin Redwoods State Park Forest Health and Resilience Project PSA/Addendum to the PEIR was prepared for the project as a later activity covered by the CalVTP EIR.

ceqa-4892b7606e00d8a6d9.name: Food Storage Lockers and Receptacles
ceqa-4892b7606e00d8a6d9.agency: California Department of Parks and Recreation
ceqa-4892b7606e00d8a6d9.description: Project proposes to install new wildlife-proof trash/recycling bins and food storage lockers (up to 145 units) at select locations throughout twenty-five (25) parks/beaches within the Santa Cruz District to replace existing non-animal proof wooden “food” lockers and non-animal waste and recycling receptacles. The new food lockers will be located within the bounds of designated sites, with final placement at the discretion of district personnel, to compensate for already existing facilities. All food lockers will meet current ADA design standards and guidelines. Installation of the new food lockers will require the excavation of one (1) 12-in. x 22-in. hole, centering the back of the food locker over the hole, attaching a pole to the container; and securing the pole in ground with quickrete. The trash receptacles will be placed on the ground and secured as needed.

ceqa-a8a23a594d15448723.name: Coastal Santa Cruz Mountains: State Parks Forest Health Initiative
ceqa-a8a23a594d15448723.agency: California Department of Parks and Recreation
ceqa-a8a23a594d15448723.description: The California Department of Parks and Recreation (California State Parks) proposes to implement vegetation treatments and maintenance treatments on up to 11,994.7 acres of land within the project area. The project area consists of the western portion of Big Basin Redwoods State Park, Año Nuevo State Park, the southern extent of Butano State Park, and various adjacent landownerships owned by the Sempervirens Fund (Cougar Ridge, Gazos 320, and Lachenbruch) and Save the Redwoods League (Cascade Creek) located in Santa Cruz and San Mateo Counties and predominately within the coastal zone. California State Parks has prepared a Project-Specific Analysis and CEQA Addendum to evaluate if the proposed project is within the scope of the California Vegetation Treatment Program EIR (CalVTP PEIR), consider revisions or changes to the PEIR that would expand its coverage to include all project areas, and provide environmental information on the proposed project. Treatment types include ecological restoration. Treatment activities include prescribed burning, manual, mechanical, and targeted herbicide application treatments. The goal of the ecologically restorative treatments proposed in this PSA/Addendum is to restore forest and shrubland conditions to exhibit an increase in healthy growth of mature vegetation while allowing for natural regeneration of understory plant species, with alignment to the San Mateo Resource Conservation District and Resource Conservation District of Santa Cruz's Forest health and Fire Resilience Program Public Works Plan goals. The Coastal Santa Cruz Mountains: State Parks Forest Health Initiative PSA/Addendum to the PEIR was prepared for the project as a later activity covered by the CalVTP PEIR.

ceqa-b9c9119174120b2343.name: Santa Cruz Resource Recovery Facility Enclosed Flare Station Installation Project
ceqa-b9c9119174120b2343.projectTitle: Santa Cruz Resource Recovery Facility Enclosed Flare Station Installation Project
ceqa-b9c9119174120b2343.description: The project consists of installation of an enclosed low-nitrogen oxide (Nox) flare to act as the backup landfill gas collection and destruction device for the existing onsite landfill gas collection system and Landfill Gas to Energy {LFGTE) Plant. The purpose of this improvement is to establish a permanent backup flare facility to collect methane gas and burn under regulatory provisions of the Monterey Bay Air Resources District (MBARD) in the event that the LFGTE is temporarily shut down. The facility would be located immediately west of the existing LFGTE Plant. The project includes construction of an approximately 3,600-square-foot flare station, which would house the low NOx flare station equipment, including the enclosed flare stack, an air compressor, three blowers, a condensate management system, and the equipment control panel. The station would be situated on a concrete pad and would be accessed by an existing landfill road. A three-foot tall concrete retaining wall would be installed on the northern boundary of the new station.

ceqa-276d993d23d207e09e.name: 2026 Regional Transportation Plan & Sustainable Communities Strategy
ceqa-276d993d23d207e09e.projectTitle: 2026 Regional Transportation Plan & Sustainable Communities Strategy
ceqa-276d993d23d207e09e.description: The proposed 2026 RTP/SCS is an update to the current 2022 RTP/SCS that was adopted in August 2022. The proposed 2026 RTP/SCS reflects changes in legislative requirements, local land use policies, and resource constraints that have occurred since adoption of the current 2022 RTP/SCS. The 2026 update to the 2022 RTP/SCS is focused on continued implementation of the 2022 RTP/SCS, with updates to ensure consistency with federal, State, and local planning requirements. As have past RTPs, the proposed 2026 RTP/SCS shows how the region can invest limited transportation funds to maintain, operate and improve an integrated, multi-modal transportation system with the purpose of facilitating the efficient movement of people and goods. The updated plan identifies specific strategies, policies, and actions, including a list of programmed and planned transportation projects feasibly within the region’s anticipated transportation funding levels, to meet the current and future needs of the region. The proposed 2026 SCS updates the 2022 SCS, adopted by TCAG in August 2022, and incorporates new strategies to address rapidly the changing regional, national, and global context with the SCS preferred scenario focusing on new development in existing urbanized infill locations and transit corridors, avoiding identified resource areas. The planning horizon of the proposed 2026 RTP/SCS is 2049.

ceqa-194a1c8a9c59d544bc.name: General Plan Amendment No. 2026-01, Change of Zone No. 2026-01 and Blankenship Phase 3 Tentative Subdivision Map No. 5610
ceqa-194a1c8a9c59d544bc.projectTitle: General Plan Amendment No. 2026-01, Change of Zone No. 2026-01 and Blankenship Phase 3 Tentative Subdivision Map No. 5610
ceqa-194a1c8a9c59d544bc.description: General Plan Amendment No. 2026-01 and Change of Zone No. 2026-01 is a request by San Joaquin Valley Homes to change the underlying land use designation of a 7.04-acre portion of an approximately 23.53 acre parcel from the existing Mixed Use Commercial (C-MU) zone and designation to Residential Low Density designation, zoned Single Family Residential (R-1). This land use designation and zoning would match the existing land use designation and zoning of the remainder of the 23.53-acre parcel. The project is supported by the accompanying request for Blankenship Phase 3 Tentative Subdivision Map No. 5610. Blankenship Phase 3 Tentative Subdivision Map No. 5610 is a request by San Joaquin Valley Homes to subdivide a 7.04-acre portion of a 23.53-acre parcel into 36 lots for single-family residential use. This will be a continuation of the existing single-family subdivision which surrounds the proposed site. The residential subdivision will meet the city’s development standards for the zone. Additionally, the project will also include the construction of streets, extension of sewer lines and laterals, future connection to the storm drainage system and extension of utilities and services (electricity, gas, water). Frontage improvements along East Caldwell Avenue including curb, gutter and parkway landscape will also be installed per city standards. Development improvements will also be included along South Santa Fe Street. The proposed site area of 7.04 acres is part of a larger 23.53-acre parcel that was included in a previous approved Annexation No. 2024-05 and Blankenship Tentative Subdivision Map No. 5602. An Initial Study was completed for that project however, at the time, the 7.04-acre commercially zoned area was not included for development and was left as a remainder for the project. Now the applicant is seeking to rezone the commercially zoned area to residential to allow for the continued development of single-family homes expanding the surrounding subdivision to include this area.

ceqa-46c86177c0d261b279.name: Mill Creek Culvert at Stevenson Street
ceqa-46c86177c0d261b279.projectTitle: Mill Creek Culvert at Stevenson Street
ceqa-46c86177c0d261b279.description: This project consists of removing and reinstalling the reinforced cast-in-place concrete culvert to improve stormwater management and protect critical infrastructure. The existing culvert along Mill Creek beneath Stevenson St is deteriorating and replacing it will reduce flood risks and enhance public safety. The improvements will benefit local residents, businesses, and first responders who rely on Stevenson St, and will prevent potential downstream property damage should the existing culvert fail.

ceqa-e37b2d47f94a1340ee.name: Tulare 198 ADA Ramps
ceqa-e37b2d47f94a1340ee.description: The proposed project will involve the replacement of two non-compliant American with Disabilities Act (ADA) curb ramps at the intersections of State Route 198 and Avenue 328 and State Route 198 and Douglas Drive in Lemon Cove, located in Tulare County. Replacing the ramps will improve accessibility for pedestrians, bring the facilities into compliance with current ADA standards, and enhance pedestrian safety.

ceqa-7a1eb713949194a0fb.name: 2026 Regional Transportation Plan & Sustainable Communities Strategy
ceqa-7a1eb713949194a0fb.projectTitle: 2026 Regional Transportation Plan & Sustainable Communities Strategy
ceqa-7a1eb713949194a0fb.description: The proposed 2026 RTP/SCS is an update to the current 2022 RTP/SCS that was adopted in August 2022. The proposed 2026 RTP/SCS reflects changes in legislative requirements, local land use policies, and resource constraints that have occurred since adoption of the current 2022 RTP/SCS. The 2026 update to the 2022 RTP/SCS is focused on continued implementation of the 2022 RTP/SCS, with updates to ensure consistency with federal, State, and local planning requirements. As have past RTPs, the proposed 2026 RTP/SCS shows how the region can invest limited transportation funds to maintain, operate and improve an integrated, multi-modal transportation system with the purpose of facilitating the efficient movement of people and goods. The updated plan identifies specific strategies, policies, and actions, including a list of programmed and planned transportation projects feasibly within the region’s anticipated transportation funding levels, to meet the current and future needs of the region. The planning horizon of the proposed 2026 RTP/SCS is 2049

ceqa-c817f7a61f404fde59.name: Woodville Farm Labor Center (WFLC) TCP Mitigation Project
ceqa-c817f7a61f404fde59.projectTitle: Woodville Farm Labor Center (WFLC) TCP Mitigation Project
ceqa-c817f7a61f404fde59.description: The proposed Project includes improvements to the existing water system. including a centralized granular activated carbon (GAC) treatment plant to treat both Well 1 and Well 3 and new pipeline. The GAC treatment plant would consist of one pair of 20,000-pound GAC treatment vessels installed on an at—grade mat foundation. A chlorination system would be added to disinfect the water after treatment utilizing a sodium hypochlorite feed system, and a sand separator and cartridge ?ltration system would be used to reduce the concentration of suspended solids reaching the GAC system. In addition to the water system improvements, including improvements to an existing storm water retention basin. a chain link fence enclosure to store sodium hypochlorite and a driveway would be added to the Project site.

ceqa-329e2b91b6217d3fd8.name: Capinero Creek Restoration Project (Restoration Management Permit No. RMP-2026-0043-R4)
ceqa-329e2b91b6217d3fd8.projectTitle: Capinero Creek Restoration Project (Restoration Management Permit No. RMP-2026-0043-R4)
ceqa-329e2b91b6217d3fd8.agency: California Department of Fish and Wildlife, Central Region 4
ceqa-329e2b91b6217d3fd8.agencyName: Fish and Wildlife, Region 4 - Central, Fresno
ceqa-329e2b91b6217d3fd8.description: On 10/5/26, the California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) issued a Restoration Management Permit (RMP) pursuant to section 1670 of the Fish and Game Code to the Tule Basin Land and Water Conservation Trust. The Project includes the implementation of varying restoration techniques to determine strategies most successful in restoring alkali desert scrub vegetative communities. CDFW has determined that the Project is a Qualifying Restoration Project pursuant to section 1671(d)(1) of the Fish and Game Code, and the Project is expected to result in a substantial, cumulative benefit to native wildlife, plants, and their habitat. This notice is to advise that CDFW issued the above-described RMP on the date signed below.

ceqa-39263254930e1af96b.description: The proposed Project is for the replacement of an existing pipeline turnout and addition of a new turnout from the TID Main Canal, establishing two separate pump and pipeline systems. The project also involves replacing two inefficient pumps and replace with new pumps.

ceqa-945242ef544337e16d.name: San Joaquin Cross Valley Loop Transmission Line Project (California Endangered Species Act Incidental Take Permit No. 2081-2013-050-04 Minor Amendment No. 7)
ceqa-945242ef544337e16d.projectTitle: San Joaquin Cross Valley Loop Transmission Project
ceqa-945242ef544337e16d.description: The ITP authorizes the construction, operation, and maintenance of a 23 mile long double-circuit 220 kilovolt (kV) transmission line looping the existing Big Creek 3-Springville transmission line to the existing Rector substation, creating the new Big Creek 3-Rector and Rector-Springville transmission line circuits. Construction was to result in impacts to 98.30 acres of California tiger salamander (Ambystoma californiense) habitat including temporary impacts to 52.62 acres and the permanent loss of 45.68 acres of California tiger salamander habitat. The activity was expected to result in incidental take of California tiger salamander, which is designated as a threatened species under the California Endangered Species Act. Construction was completed in late 2014 and the Minor Amendment No. 7 (Amendment) includes one change to the ITP as originally issued: an extension of an additional 60 months allowed for the mitigation obligation to be fulfilled.

ceqa-ed1569cf4a098c9f5d.name: Tulare County Roadside Hazardous Fuels Control Project
ceqa-ed1569cf4a098c9f5d.projectTitle: Tulare County Roadside Hazardous Fuels Control Project
ceqa-ed1569cf4a098c9f5d.description: The County proposes a five-year roadside hazardous fuels reduction program. Work will occur along approximately 400 miles of existing County road rights-of-way in High and Very High Fire Hazard Severity areas and will be limited to a 30-foot roadside treatment buffer. Treatments include removal of small vegetation and ladder fuels; selective removal of hazardous woody vegetation, trees, and shrubs up to 18 inches in diameter within or overhanging the rightof-way; weed abatement by pulling, mowing, or lawful herbicide application; and chipping, with chipped material scattered to a depth of less than four inches or removed. Treatment is intended for gentle slopes of less than 20 percent. Work will be performed by County staff and contracted crews. The purpose is to reduce hazardous fuel loads, maintain safer evacuation and emergency-response corridors, protect public infrastructure, and improve ingress and egress for residents and first responders. No roadway widening, new travel lanes, or new roads are proposed. Beneficiaries of the Project are community members and roadway users in mountainous areas of Tulare County.

ceqa-7aba7f91da3c7746b5.name: Tulare 190 Preservation
ceqa-7aba7f91da3c7746b5.description: The project proposes to build new sidewalks with Americans with Disabilities Act ramps in the town of Springville. Along with cold planing the existing pavement from post miles 32.17 to 52.80. Work also includes installation of rumble strips, replacing existing traffic stripes, upgrading roadside signs and Metal Beam Guardrails, installing and replacing Vehicle Detection Systems, and upgrading drainage systems but replacing and repairing culverts. The purpose is to restore the existing facility to a state of good serviceability.

ceqa-0d4c211299555fb100.name: Kennedy Meadows Roadside Fuels Reduction Project
ceqa-0d4c211299555fb100.projectTitle: Kennedy Meadows Roadside Fuels Reduction Project
ceqa-0d4c211299555fb100.description: The Project will reduce hazardous roadside vegetation along approximately 3 miles of Sherman Pass Road to improve life safety, roadside safety, ingress and egress for evacuation, and reduce the intensity and spread of wildland fire into the wildland-urban interface. Tulare County Fire Department Type II IA crews will physically remove and/or chip vegetation along the roadway right-of-way and adjacent properties. All work will be within the County Right-of-way and will extend no further than 80 feet from centerline of roadway, creating a 160-foot wide (including the road) reduction of fuel, where access is authorized. Sherman Pass Road is County maintained, is located within the State Responsibility Area, and portions of the project corridor extend through the Sequoia National Forest. The roadway is in a Very High Fire Hazard Severity Zone and serves as the primary ingress and egress route for approximately 200 habitable residential structures. The Project also includes public outreach intended to improve community wildfire safety and readiness.

ceqa-e1493ee9e14f520d25.name: Tulare County Behavioral Health Residential Campus Project
ceqa-e1493ee9e14f520d25.projectTitle: Tulare County Behavioral Health Residential Campus Project
ceqa-e1493ee9e14f520d25.description: The 2.72-acre site is the former Casa Grande Assisted Living Facility and contains two existing buildings, onsite parking, and an unimproved area. The County acquired the property in 2023 and proposes to renovate and repurpose the existing campus as the Tulare County Behavioral Health Residential Campus to provide inpatient/residential behavioral health and supportive services. In addition to renovation and reuse of the existing facilities, Building 2 would be expanded by approximately 4,480 square feet on the south end of the building. The preliminary plans identify Building 2 as approximately 24,360 square feet following the addition. The current action includes program funding, renovation/conversion, the Building 2 addition, and operation of the existing campus.

ceqa-34ba856dfe89ef2fe6.name: Upper Posey Roadside Fuels Reduction Project
ceqa-34ba856dfe89ef2fe6.projectTitle: Upper Posey Roadside Fuels Reduction Project
ceqa-34ba856dfe89ef2fe6.description: The Project will reduce hazardous roadside vegetation along approximately 3.9 miles of Mountain Road 3 (Old Stage Road) and Guhl Avenue. Tulare County Fire Department Type IIA crews will thin, prune/limb, chip, and remove hazardous fuels along existing roadway corridors. Hazard trees may be removed; within fuelreduction areas, trees less than 12 inches DBH may be removed, remaining trees may be limbed to approximately 6 feet, and approximately 70 percent of standing brush may be removed, with a target stem spacing of approximately 16 feet. All work will be within the County Right-of-way and will extend no further than 80 feet from centerline of roadway, creating a 160-foot wide (including the road) reduction of fuel. The Project will improve emergency access and evacuation, reduce wildfire intensity and spread, and help protect approximately 317 homes and 982 residents in a Very High Fire Hazard Severity Zone.

ceqa-05689519be90fea180.name: Woodville Elementary Pedestrian Improvements Project
ceqa-05689519be90fea180.description: The project consists of constructing ADA compliant curb ramps, sidewalks, curb and gutters and driveways adjacent to Woodville Elementary School in the community of Woodville.

ceqa-c02bcf84d08a084ef0.name: Bardsley Avenue Sidewalk Improvements
ceqa-c02bcf84d08a084ef0.description: The project addresses a safety concern regarding the discontinuous sidewalk section on the north side of Bardsley at Morrison St., on the east and west sides. The project will install an ADA-complaint sidewalk.

ceqa-4f57447d805015afac.name: Wiersma RV and Mini Storage (GPA 26-001 & PZC 25-011)
ceqa-4f57447d805015afac.projectTitle: Wiersma RV and Mini Storage (GPA 26-001 & PZC 25-011)
ceqa-4f57447d805015afac.description: The applicant proposes Zone Change No. PZC 25-011 to change the existing zoning for APNs: 073-140-045 & 047 from the Exclusive Agriculture – 40 Acre Minimum (AE-40) Zone to the Service Commercial with a Mixed Use Overlay Zone (C-3-MU). The Tulare County Resource Management Agency (RMA) proposes General Plan Amendment No. GPA 26-001 to amend Part II: Figure 2-1 of the Corridors Framework Plan of the Tulare County General Plan 2030 Update to change the segment of State Route 198 (SR-198) between Road 64 and the Kings/Tulare County Border (Road 44) from a Major Roadway to a Regional Growth Corridor. GPA 26-001 also proposes to change the land use designation from Valley Agriculture to Mixed Use. The property currently contains an existing 3.8 acre walnut dehydrator facility, an approximately 7.71 acre walnut orchard, and 5.69 acres of fallow land on the 17.20 acre property. Existing structures on the property include a 30 foot by 40 foot tool storage shop addition; a 40 foot by 120 foot open cover with 20 foot by 40 foot enclosed for storage; a 30 foot by 66 foot shade cover to existing shade for ag equipment; a polyethylene gas line to supply natural gas to (3) nut dryers, piping, electrical and anchoring equipment; a 35 foot wide commercial asphalt concrete drive approach to Tulare County Improvement Standards, Plate A-17 and A-17C, starting 17 feet west of the center line of Road 52 and 519 feet north of the center line of SR-198; a 30 foot by 60 foot shade addition to existing shade cover for Walnut Dehydrator Facility; and a 1,200 square foot metal storage building. The purpose of the application would be to facilitate the establishment of a 3.6 acre RV Storage Facility with 160 spaces, a 440 Square Foot Office/2,087 Square Foot Residence with a 1,002 Square Foot Garage, and a 9.6 acre Future Mini-Storage Facility because there is no longer water to farm the 17.20 acre property. The existing walnut dehydrator would continue to operate. The new facilities would be added to the existing walnut dehydrator facility, which would continue to operate. However, the 7.71 acre walnut orchard that is on the property will be removed due to the lack of water to continue farming the property. The property doesn’t have access to surface water. The proposed facility will operate every day from 7:00 AM to 6:00 PM. It will be fully fenced and gated to ensure security. Additionally, an office and residence will be located on-site to provide oversight and maintenance, though there will be no full-time employees. A designated retention basin will be utilized for rainwater runoff, complying with local environmental requirements. Access to the site would be from Road 52. The applicants believe that the proposed facility will serve the growing storage needs of the community while aligning with Tulare County’s zoning and development standards. The applicants have stated that they are prepared to comply with all necessary permits and regulations to ensure a seamless approval process.

ceqa-1236e4b6f8f1685640.name: Extension of Uncodified Urgency Interim Ordinance No. 3669 - Temporary Moratorium on New Data Center Development
ceqa-1236e4b6f8f1685640.projectTitle: Extension of Uncodified Urgency Interim Ordinance No. 3669 - Temporary Moratorium on New Data Center Development
ceqa-1236e4b6f8f1685640.description: The County of Tulare is extending Uncodified Urgency Interim Ordinance No. 3669, which establishes a temporary moratorium on new data center development in the unincorporated areas of Tulare County. The extension will continue the moratorium for an additional ten (10) months and fifteen (15) days, through August 6, 2027. During the moratorium, the County will continue to evaluate data center development and develop comprehensive land use regulations addressing potential impacts and appropriate development standards, including zoning requirements, infrastructure needs, environmental considerations, public safety, water and energy considerations, noise, and land use compatibility. The purpose of the moratorium extension is to allow sufficient time for the County to complete this evaluation and develop appropriate permanent zoning and development regulations governing new data center development. The residents and communities of unincorporated Tulare County, as well as the County generally, will benefit from the additional time to evaluate and establish appropriate land use regulations for future data center development.

ceqa-c2de5d7e0585a1a57a.name: Deer Creek Stream Gauge Vegetation Removal
ceqa-c2de5d7e0585a1a57a.projectTitle: Deer Creek Stream Gauge Vegetation Removal
ceqa-c2de5d7e0585a1a57a.description: Hand tools and a weed eater will be used to remove vegetation within the dry channel, from the levee road to the current waterline, and 10 feet upstream and downstream of the station. The work is to maintain proper access to and operation of the station. Local farmers, residents, and local jurisdictions will benefit from monitoring stream flow and flood warning.

ceqa-5b70102421b779c155.name: Tentative Parcel Map No. PPM 26-022
ceqa-5b70102421b779c155.description: The applicant is requesting allow the division of approximately 86.13 acres into two parcels with a Waived Final Map: Proposed Parcel No. 1 = 1.08 acres, and Proposed Parcel No. 2 = 85.05 acres. The subject site is within the AE-40 (Exclusive Agricultural 40 Acre Minimum) Zone with a Land Use Designation of Valley Agricultural, in the Rural Valley Lands Plan. Subsection D.2.g. of Section 15 of the Tulare County Zoning Ordinance (TCZO) states division is allowable if property has less than the minimum acreage if, "a homesite parcel may be created for the purpose of separating an existing residence or mobilehome from the remaining agricultural portion of the site. If the parcel of record to be divided is greater in size than is required in the zone district in which it is located, a maximum of one (1) homesite parcel shall be permitted The proposed project would authorize one additional residence for the property owners and/or their family and would not authorize expansion of agricultural operations, or any other use unless separately reviewed and approved by the County.

ceqa-4137c8f16c94a6527c.name: Project Title: Cardoza Contractor Storage Yard (PSP 26-013)
ceqa-4137c8f16c94a6527c.description: The applicant proposes the establishment and operation of a contractor storage yard to support an off-site landscaping business. Development of the site includes construction of a 3,600-square-foot metal shop building, installation of an on-site wastewater treatment/septic system, and graveled access road. The contractor storage yard would accommodate parking and storage of up to twelve pickup trucks, twelve cargo or flatbed trailers, lawn maintenance equipment and mowers, employee parking, and associated site access and circulation improvements necessary for daily operations. An Initial Study (IS) was prepared by the Environmental Planning Division of the Resource Management Agency (RMA) for PSP 26-013, identifying potentially significant environmental effects associated with the project. A Mitigated Negative Declaration (MND) and Mitigation Monitoring and Reporting Program (MMRP) were subsequently prepared, concluding that although the project may have the potential to significantly affect the environment, the incorporation of mitigation measures would reduce all impacts to levels where no significant effect would occur, and no substantial evidence exists indicating that the revised project would result in significant impacts. The MND (SCH #2026080007) describes these mitigation measures and explains how they reduce potential effects to lessthan- significant levels, as supported by the environmental checklist prepared pursuant to the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). Based on the analysis in the Initial Study and accompanying technical documentation, all potential impacts—including Biological Resources; Cultural, Tribal, and Paleontological Resources; Geology and Soils; and Noise—were determined to be less than significant or less than significant with mitigation incorporated.

ceqa-fcd288009d6fd140b1.projectTitle: Kern River No. 3 Culvert Replacement Project (Notification of Lake or Streambed Alteration, No. EPIMS-TUL-62019-R4)

ceqa-f73993fbb79eb15d89.name: Tipton Community Services District Well No. 6 Equipping and Distribution System Connection Project
ceqa-f73993fbb79eb15d89.projectTitle: Tipton Community Services District Well No. 6 Equipping and Distribution System Connection Project
ceqa-f73993fbb79eb15d89.description: The proposed Project consists of equipping a previously drilled well with a pump and associated appurtenances and connecting the well to the Tipton Community Services District's existing water distribution system. Work will include installation of a 75-horsepower well pump equipped with a variable-frequency drive (VFD) and related appurtenances, construction of approximately 30 feet of piping to connect the well to the existing distribution system, and minor trenching and backfilling as necessary. Construction is expected to take approximately 20 working days. Once completed, the previously drilled well will be available to supply water through the District's existing municipal water system. The Project would improve the reliability and redundancy of the District’s existing water system and would not expand the District’s service area or provide water for a specific development project. No new well drilling is proposed. The Project would occur at the site of an existing, previously drilled municipal well and would involve a limited area of temporary ground disturbance. Disturbed surfaces would be restored following installation. The Project would not affect a designated sensitive environmental resource, scenic highway, hazardous-waste site identified pursuant to Government Code section 65962.5, or historical resource. There are no unusual circumstances associated with the project that would create a reasonable possibility of a significant environmental effect, and the project would not contribute to a significant cumulative impact from successive projects of the same type in the same place. Therefore, none of the exceptions in CEQA Guidelines section 15300.2 applies.

ceqa-47ab42659e295f6ca7.description: The Applicant, Sierra View Dairy, is requesting approval to allow for the construction and operation of an anaerobic digester, a biogas conditioning plant, and a low-pressure biogas pipeline for connection to an existing biogas collection and upgrading system and will not change or increase the amount of permitted animal units on this existing dairy site. The beneficiary of the project is the Applicant.

ceqa-5c7ffb1d2942555bbc.name: Visalia Landfill Scale Expansion Project
ceqa-5c7ffb1d2942555bbc.description: The Visalia Landfill Scale Expansion Project scope of work includes adding a new gate entrance, installing approximately 16,000 square feet (sf) of asphalt concrete paving, and installing electrical and low voltage infrastructure for a new scale weigh station. The added infrastructure will be within the limits of the existing landfill facility. This added infrastructure once completed will have beneficial impacts. The new entrance will allow expedited entrance for commercial trucks that use the landfill on a regular basis. The commercial trucks will have radio frequency identification (RFID) tags that will record the truck weight upon entrance into the facility. With this new system the commercial trucks will not need to weigh a second time when exiting the facility. The overall truck wait time, and idle time will be reduced thus reducing vehicle emissions and improving the efficiency of the facility operations.

ceqa-f0005106ce8ceebac6.name: Seaborn Reservoir Project
ceqa-f0005106ce8ceebac6.description: Alternative A – Seaborn Reservoir Alternative A would consist of developing an internal storage reservoir in an abandoned aggregate mining operation where surface water can be re-regulated (filled and emptied) for use by the Project Owners. The Project would be located on the Seaborn Property approximately one mile southeast of the City of Woodlake. The centroid of the Project is 36°23’39.62” N, 119°4’1.87” W. The approximately 235-acres water storage facility equipped with a bidirectional pipeline, an inlet/outlet structure at McKays Point, an outlet structure into the St. Johns River, and a pump station (see Figure 1). Water diverted from the Kaweah River at McKays Point will flow by gravity through a new pipeline to the Seaborn Reservoir across the adjacent property, which is also owned by the Property Owners. Conveyance features would be installed in the southeast corner of the reservoir area to deliver water to and from the St. Johns River and Kaweah River for use by the Project Owners. The area surrounding the internal reservoir would be restored as a habitat area, including native plants and riparian habitat. Restoration of the habitat area would be completed in collaboration with an entity that specializes in habitat restoration. During construction, non-native plants would be removed, and native plant species would be preserved to the greatest extent feasible. Alternative B-- Kaweah Return Location Alternative B would include all of the same features as Alternative A except the water outlet would be due south to the Kaweah River rather than returning water at the McKays Point Structure. This alternative would also be 290 acres and would include a water storage facility equipped with a pipeline, an inlet at McKays Point, and an outlet that would flow into the Kaweah River (see Figure 1). Water diverted from the Kaweah River at McKays Point would flow via gravity through a new pipeline toward the Seaborn Reservoir. Conveyance features would be installed in the southeast corner of the reservoir to deliver water to and from the Kaweah River for use by the Project Owners. The pipeline south to the Kaweah River for pumped return water is anticipated to require less vertical elevation across the pipeline than in Alternative A, which could potentially lessen long-term pumping costs. All other features associated with Alternative B would be the same as in Alternative A. Alternative C – Land Fallowing Alternative C would not require construction or alter the existing land in the Project area and would instead improve water supply through land fallowing. Land fallowing is a practice that involves leaving farmland unplanted for a year or more to conserve water supplies, particularly groundwater. Some benefits associated with land fallowing include soil restoration, and water conservation. To achieve the target water volume, nearly 2,200 acres (assuming a demand of 3 acre-feet per acre) would need to be fallowed. While Alternative C would reduce water demand, it would not result in the distribution of captured water supply to the Project Owners’ service area. This Alternative would also not provide any flood reduction benefits.

ceqa-cb9f1fee4c41bbc92e.name: Grants Check Structure Project
ceqa-cb9f1fee4c41bbc92e.description: The District proposes to reconstruct a failed water flow regulating structure within the St. Johns River. A new concrete pad will be installed for the placement of the pneumatically actuated gates, which will span the entire width of the existing St. Johns River channel on the new concrete pad. The gate system relies on an airbladder to inflate and raise or deflate and lower the gate system and is composed of a gate panel, anchoring system, air bladder, hinge flap, clamp casting, seals, and retraining straps. The Project will be designed to meet the flow capacity of 8,000 cubic feet per second. The pneumatic gate is designed to be low maintenance, allowing large debris, tree logs or stumps to pass with flowing water without any blockage. The gates will allow the flow to be regulated during normal operations by inflating the air bladder. The concrete pad will be designed to allow heavy equipment like excavators and trucks to access the gates in the event of an emergency. The gates and air bladder will only be accessible during dry seasons or when there is no flow in the river channel. Construction is anticipated to take 180 days and will occur when the St. Johns River is largely dry.

ceqa-f35388550919653de3.name: RPCA Solar 17, LLC Project (PSP 25-092)
ceqa-f35388550919653de3.description: The proposed solar energy generation facility is located in unincorporated Tulare County just north of Porterville on approximately 13.6 acres of three parcels totaling 17.6 acres (APN 243-090-037, 243-090-092, and 243-090-093; Figure 1). The Project area is situated at elevations ranging between approximately 420 to 430 feet above mean sea level (AMSL). Avenue 182 (Ave 182) and State Route 65 (SR 65) bisects the [JW1.1]middle lower third of the Project area, with two parcels situated north of the road and one parcel situated to the south (Figure 2). The two northern parcels are bounded to the west by the Friant-Kern Canal, to the northeast by State Route 65, and to the south by Ave 182Road 232. The southern parcel is bounded to the north Ave 182and east by Road 232, and by rural residential parcels to the south and west. Land surrounding the Project area consists of agricultural land and scattered rural residential properties. The Project area is situated in Section 9 of Township 21 South and Range 27 East within the Porterville, California 7.5-minute U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) quadrangle. The corresponding latitude and longitude at the approximate center of the Project area is 36°07’16.35” north latitude and -119°03’20.95” west longitude. The proposed small-scale utility solar generation project is located in the Exclusive Agricultural “AE” zoning district. RPCA Solar 17, LLC (sponsor/applicant) has entered into a long-term lease agreement with the property owner, the Antoine Bechara Revocable Trust, to facilitate the development and long-term operation of the Project. When complete, the Project will generate up to 3 megawatts (MW) of alternating current (AC) clean, reliable solar energy. The Project will interconnect to Southern California Edison’s (SCE) pre-existing electrical distribution system adjacent to the site. The power generated from this facility is expected to be sold to the Clean Power Alliance through a long-term Power Purchase Agreement (PPA). The Project will utilize solar modules to convert the sun’s energy into usable (AC) power. Single-axis tracking technology will be utilized to allow the modules to efficiently track the sun throughout the day and maximize the efficiency of solar collection. The rows of modules will be anchored in the ground using driven piles, and the approximate height of the array is 8 feet, and the maximum height of the array will not exceed 15 feet above ground at maximum tilt. The Project will be fenced in with a six-foot chain-link fence with a foot of straight wire on top for a total fence height of approximately seven feet. A minimal opening of no more than 1one foot may be provided at the base of the fence at appropriate intervals as a wildlife-permeable design. The Project sites and panel arrays would be accessed via an all-weather gravel road that surrounds both sections of the Project area and is approximately 20 feet wide and over 5,000 feet in length. Electric power connections will be provided via existing overhead power lines adjacent to Ave 182/Road 232 in the middle of the Project site. Approximately 50 feet from Ave 182/Road 232, these overhead power lines will transition to power pole connections and then underground utility runs adjacent to the access road. Utility connections will be underground from this point to the power station and transformer located in the middle of the project area. The Project will require minimal regularly planned maintenance and will be operated remotely. The Project sponsor will enter into an operations and maintenance contractor[JW2.1] to provide proper operation and maintenance of the facility; and general maintenance of the Project grounds. Native groundcover restoration and maintenance after installation will provide increased site drainage and groundwater percolation and limit sheet flows out of the project area. No firearms or pets will be allowed on the site during construction of the Project or during ongoing operations and maintenance activities. All heavy equipment and vehicles used during Project construction will be washed prior to mobilization to the site to prevent the spread of noxious weeds. Construction equipment will be cleaned of mud or other debris that may contain invasive plants and/or seeds and inspected to reduce the potential for spreading noxious weeds. All mitigation measures will be incorporated into the Mitigation Monitoring and Reporting Program developed for the Project, and the Applicant will implement all monitoring and reporting obligations as detailed in this IS/MND.

ceqa-1b24522135661ad76e.name: Former Lamoure’s Cleaners and Former Country Club Cleaners Visalia Dry Cleaner Investigation Project Removal Action Work Plan – Soil and Soil Vapor
ceqa-1b24522135661ad76e.projectTitle: Former Lamoure’s Cleaners and Former Country Club Cleaners Visalia Dry Cleaner Investigation Project Removal Action Work Plan – Soil and Soil Vapor
ceqa-1b24522135661ad76e.agency: California Department of Toxic Substances Control
ceqa-1b24522135661ad76e.description: The project includes installing and operating a soil vapor extraction (SVE) system at the former Lamoure’s and Former Country Club Cleaners properties to address soil and soil vapor impacts by volatile organic compounds (VOCs), primarily tetrachloroethene (PCE), presumed to have resulted from spills and other handling processes from several former dry-cleaning facilities. The project is anticipated to take approximately seven years at the former Lamoure’s site and three months over a one-year period at the former Country Club site. Remediation activities include: • Construct and install full-scale and temporary soil vapor extraction (SVE) systems, including SVE wells, nested soil vapor probes, and below-ground polyvinyl chloride (PVC) conveyance piping at the former Lamoure’s Cleaners and Country Club Cleaners properties. • Air/dust controls and monitoring during construction: implementation of temporary stormwater management best management practices (BMPs), and dust control measures. • Site security and implementation measures (Traffic Control Plan (TCP), and a Site-specific Health and Safety Plan (HASP)). In addition, Mitigation Measure NOI-1 (Operational Noise Reduction) is implemented to address potential noise impacts and ensure compliance with City of Visalia Ordinance 8.36.040. • Preparation of a Construction Completion Report documenting completion of removal action activities. • Finalize and implement an Operation, Maintenance, and Monitoring (OM&M) manual for each SVE system.

ceqa-a9fb3d0fbf34cd4923.name: 2026 Road Repair and Accountability Act (RRAA) Project 1
ceqa-a9fb3d0fbf34cd4923.projectTitle: 2026 Road Repair and Accountability Act (RRAA) Project 1
ceqa-a9fb3d0fbf34cd4923.description: The Project consists of repairing asphalt materials on multiple segments of existing County roads. The work includes a combination of isolated pavement repairs followed by the installation of new asphalt surfacing. All projects will include corrective work (adding a thin course of granular material for leveling to minimize drop-off heights for overlays) to be performed on the shoulders of the roadways. Furthermore, all newly surfaced roadways will receive new traffic stripes and pavement markings. Efficient and responsive improvements and maintenance of the County road network will enhance the safety and security of the public by improving the access of pedestrians and the transportation infrastructure for the general population throughout the region. Construction is anticipated to begin during the third quarter through the fourth quarter of 2026. The beneficiaries of the Project include users of the County roads.

ceqa-2a083dcb5bd3ff5ad9.name: One-Way STOP Control on Avenue 404 at Road 64, southwest of Dinuba
ceqa-2a083dcb5bd3ff5ad9.projectTitle: One-Way STOP Control on Avenue 404 at Road 64, southwest of Dinuba
ceqa-2a083dcb5bd3ff5ad9.description: This project will enhance vehicular circulation and traffic safety at the intersection of Avenue 404 and Road 64, and will consist of installing a One-Way Stop sign on Avenue 404 at Road 64, located southwest of the incorporated City of Dinuba, CA. This "T" intersection is currently uncontrolled, with no posted Stop sign. In response to concerns regarding traffic safety, the Tulare County Resource Management Agency (RMA) conducted an investigation. To improve the vehicular circulation and safety at this intersection, the Traffic Operations Division determined that this intersection meets the requirements of Section 2B.04 Right of Way at Intersections of the California Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (CA MUTCD), and is consistent with the California Vehicle Code (CVC), Section 22450(c), which states in part that “a local authority may adopt rules and regulations by ordinance or resolution providing for the placement of a stop sign at any location on a highway under its jurisdiction where the stop sign would enhance traffic safety”.

ceqa-cb07a8ef37095724b0.name: 2026 Slurry Seal Program
ceqa-cb07a8ef37095724b0.description: The 2026 Slurry Seal Program Project consists of slurry sealing approximately 9 miles of existing County roads within unincorporated communities in Tulare County, including road segments in or near South Visalia Area, Ivanhoe, North/South Porterville Area, Springville, Pixley, and Strathmore. The work would occur on existing paved roadways, including road segments within subdivisions with curb and gutter. The purpose of the Project is to preserve and protect the underlying pavement structure, extend pavement service life, and provide a renewed driving surface for users of these facilities. The Project would not add automobile travel lanes or expand roadway capacity. Construction is anticipated to begin in the third quarter of 2026 and be completed in the fourth quarter of 2026.

ceqa-164a7e7983378813df.name: Avenue 56 Permanent Restoration Improvements Project
ceqa-164a7e7983378813df.description: Avenue 56 serves as a major collector road from the community of Alpaugh to State Routes 43 and 99. ceqa-6c99598ff0e3ea8070.name: MHDSF Winter HQ Fuel Reduction
ceqa-6c99598ff0e3ea8070.agency: California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection
ceqa-6c99598ff0e3ea8070.agencyName: Forestry and Fire Protection, Department of
ceqa-6c99598ff0e3ea8070.description: The proposed project will involve fuel reduction activities on 30 acres of state and 50 acres of adjoining private property. The project location ranges in elevation from 3,680-4,400 feet. The vegetation type of the project area is an oak woodland forest community. The overstory consists of ponderosa pine (Pinus ponderosa), incense-cedar (Calocedrus decurrens), California black oak (Quercus kelloggii), and interior live oak (Quercus wislizeni). The understory consists of white leaf manzanita (Arctostaphylos viscida), buckbrush (Ceanothus cuneatus), deerbrush (Ceanothus integerrimus), California buckeye (Aesculus californica), and western poison-oak (Toxicodendron diversilobum). Project work will reduce hazardous fuel loads by removal of underbrush, and dead, dying and diseased vegetation. Project activities will be completed by hand crews and include thinning of brush and shrubs; thinning and limbing of small trees; removal of dead material; piling and burning of cut biomass material. No heavy equipment will be used during this project.

ceqa-dd43ab9c934236d4e8.name: Tulare County Stream Channel Routine Maintenance Agreement Project
ceqa-dd43ab9c934236d4e8.projectTitle: Tulare County Stream Channel Routine Maintenance Agreement Project
ceqa-dd43ab9c934236d4e8.description: Tulare County proposes to enter into a long-term 12-year Streambed Alteration Agreement with the California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) for ongoing implementation of routine maintenance activities within jurisdictional improved and unimproved stream channels and drainage facilities, and associated CDFW jurisdictional areas throughout the County. The County anticipates completing approximately 30 maintenance projects per year over the 12-year life of the agreement. Routine maintenance activities may include removal, replacement, or repair of drainage facilities; channel alignment maintenance; debris or obstruction removal; silt, sand, gravel, or sediment removal under dry conditions; vegetation control in channels or on banks; goat/sheep grazing for vegetation and thatch management; minor erosion control work; repair of previous erosion control work; and geotechnical sampling or subsurface cultural resource sensitivity testing. Exact methods, locations, and the extent of individual maintenance activities would be submitted to CDFW for review and approval through the Verification Request Form process.

ceqa-360eb3e17cd9b696aa.name: Windy Springs Meadow Restoration
ceqa-360eb3e17cd9b696aa.agency: California Regional Water Quality Control Board, Central Valley Fresno Region 5
ceqa-360eb3e17cd9b696aa.agencyName: Regional Water Quality Control Board, Region 5 - Fresno
ceqa-360eb3e17cd9b696aa.description: The 2.99-acre Project consists of correcting the hydrologic alterations to Windy Springs Meadow caused by historical ranching infrastructure, channelization, and meadow berm construction. The Project will restore the natural hydrologic and ecological functions of Windy Springs Meadow, its associated springs, and the intermittent tributary that flows through the meadow. Work includes removing artificial containment structures from two springheads, reestablishing the natural spring outflow channel through localized bank grading and cobble placement, and lowering or removing two man made berms to restore surface sheet flow and expand wetland hydrology. Salvaged meadow sod and native vegetation will be reused to stabilize disturbed soils and fill shallow anthropogenic depressions.

ceqa-d7ac1ca672614f343d.name: Emergency Permit for Management of Hazardous Waste, EMD Millipore Sigma Company, Visalia, California
ceqa-d7ac1ca672614f343d.projectTitle: Emergency Permit for Management of Hazardous Waste, EMD Millipore Sigma Company, Visalia, California
ceqa-d7ac1ca672614f343d.agency: California Department of Toxic Substances Control
ceqa-d7ac1ca672614f343d.description: The California Department of Toxic Substances Control (DTSC), pursuant to authority granted under California Code of Regulations (CCR), Title 22, Division 4.5, Chapter 20, Sec. 66270.61, has issued an Emergency Permit to the EMD Millipore Sigma Company, (EPA ID# CAR000301093) to treat hazardous wastes through a controlled reaction with chemical solutions. Specifically, thirty eight (38) 1-liter containers, two (2) 100-milliliter containers, four (4) 4-liter containers, and three (3) 500-milliliter containers of Diethyl Ether; six (6) 100-milliliter containers of Cyclophenyl Methyl Ether; one (1) 500-milliliter container of Diisopropyl Ether; thirty four (34) 1-liter containers, one (1) 500-milliliter container, and twelve (12) 100-milliliter containers of Tetrahydrofuran; two (2) 1-liter containers and one (1) 4-liter container of 1,4 Dioxane; thirteen (13) 100-gram containers, one (1) 200-gram container, one (1) 1-liter container, and six (6) 500-milliliter containers of Acrylic Acid; one (1) 2-liter container of Styrene and two (2) 500-milliliter containers of Styrene; four (4) 2-liter containers of Methyl Methacrylate; and one (1) 500-gram container of Benzoyl Peroxide must be stabilized prior to transport to an authorized hazardous waste treatment, storage, and disposal facility. These chemicals are currently being stored at EMD Millipore Sigma Company located at 8511 West Riggin Avenue, Visalia, California. DTSC has determined as a safety precaution to prevent an accident or severe injury, an Emergency Permit should be issued to chemically stabilize the hazardous wastes by Clean Harbors Environmental Services (Clean Harbors) prior to storage and eventual transportation off-site. Background: One hundred thirty-two (132) containers have peroxide formation present on either the inside, outside, or the bottom of the chemicals’ containers, as well as the thread container caps. The presence of peroxide formation may be unstable at relatively low concentrations, resulting in fire and/or explosion if improperly handled. One (1) container has shock and/or temperature sensitive materials that can decompose or detonate with external energy when dry or concentrated. If the material is improperly handled, there is a potential for a reaction, which includes fire, deflagration, or detonation. Due to the presence of peroxide formation/shock-sensitive materials, DTSC considers these chemicals to be an imminent and substantial endangerment to human health and the environment. Chemical stabilization is recommended prior to transport to a permitted treatment, storage, and disposal facility. Project Activities: The treatment of these hazardous wastes involves the addition of solutions to the containers in a controlled manner to reduce the reactive or ignitable characteristics of the chemicals. Treatment will take place within a designated exclusion zone. Only technicians from Clean Harbors will be allowed in the exclusion zone. Movement, preparation, and treatment of the containers will be in accordance with established standards. Within 10 business days of the expiration of this permit, EMD Millipore Sigma Company will submit a final report, signed in accordance with Title 22, CCR Sec. 66270.11(d). The report shall include certification that the treatment area has been cleared of all residual hazardous waste generated from this emergency treatment and all generated waste has been properly managed. The Emergency Permit is effective beginning July 23, 2026 and shall expire on October 20, 2026.

ceqa-a9cfe204ee1ea86e5e.name: Clements Ranch Tentative Tract Map No. 5606
